sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.text: We spent most of SN5 machining molds on the Jacobs Shopbot's daily slot scramble, right up until Jacobs staff pulled us aside for block-reserving (2026-02-23). That's not a conversation we want to have twice (PP-06). We now machine on the ShopSabre at RFS, with our own reservation system, a 5×10 ft bed, vacuum hold-down, and an automatic tool changer. This doc covers how to book it, who can run it, and the setup rules that cost us parts when we skipped them.

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.text: Machining polyurethane tooling-board molds and stock on the RFS ShopSabre. The same booking, operator and Z-zero rules apply to XPS foam (wing cores), G10 and cured CF panels cut on the ShopSabre. G10 runs only with Larry's say-so. CF and G10 dust is handled per CS-009. The Jacobs Shopbot is still fine as a fallback for small jobs; use the SN5 *Shopbot Procedure Checklist* there (that machine has none of the features below; everything is manual).

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.text:
- **HOT**: RFS hands-on-training sign-off; required before you run the machine on your own.
- **Certified operator**: did the RFS ShopSabre training doc + HOT. RFS's own record, on the RSO/RFS student access dashboard, is the authority. The app's ShopSabre CNC training (People tab) mirrors it: a lead grants it only after seeing the member's RFS record. The app will not let anyone without it sign Machine mold, except a lead who presses Sign without it and writes a reason, which the app records on the work order (`app/workorders.js`). The end-of-SN5 list (Ansh, Simon, Kina, Nico, Nick, Justin, Sam, Alvin, Ernesto) is history, not a roster. Re-check who's still around each fall and train replacements early, October not February.
- **CAM review**: Larry requires whoever is machining to have made their own CAM, and he reviews it before it runs. Build this into the schedule; it has saved us more than it has cost us.
- **ATC**: automatic tool changer. The machine swaps tools from its rack mid-program and measures each tool's length automatically, so tool changes don't need a manual re-zero.

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.text:
- **Machine:** hands away from a live spindle; know where the e-stop is before every run; watch the first minutes with a hand near it. Max 2 people at the machine during setup (kept from the Shopbot rules; still a good rule).
- **Tooling-board dust:** abrasive and irritating. Extraction on, dust mask minimum (respirator for long jobs). Vacuum shared rooms; don't blow dust around with compressed air.
- **Eyes:** safety glasses at the machine whenever the spindle runs or you clear chips (R6 §8: standard safety glasses).
- **Vacuum table:** don't reach under a held part to "check" it while zones are on; release zones first.

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.text:
1. When mold CAM starts (not when it finishes), write the machining time estimate in the work order's Machine mold step note (Glue and machine mold on a wet-layup run; there is no estimate field) and book the slot on the RFS/RSO site (R1). Our SN5 UT molds ran 0:17–6:16 each; CAM simulation gets you a real number.
2. Book under the name of whoever is actually running the machine. RFS rule: you attend your own reservation. No covering slots for each other; that's the exact thing that burned us at Jacobs.
3. Booking-site quirks (as of spring 2026): multi-day and some short blocks fail: book day-by-day chunks and report bugs to Joey.
4. Put the job in a ShopSabre slot row (ShopSabre slot 1 or ShopSabre slot 2) on the Schedule tab, Season by station view. The row is the team's plan and does not reserve the machine; step 1 does. The weekly meeting reviews the next 2 weeks of machine load, so conflicts show up there, not at the machine.
5. The stack plan, and the blanks used as CAM stock, come from CS-003 §7.1 steps 8 and 9 (the app's planner or the FEBPlanStock Fusion add-in).

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.text:
1. Certified operator, running their own CAM, reviewed by Larry (R1).
2. Mold design review initialed on the WO (CS-003 §7.2). No initials, no machining.
3. Stock glued/cured per CS-003 §7.3 and labeled, and check the label is actually the job you booked. The mold is at Board glued in the app.
4. The mold's Mold file is the current plan, not one marked Superseded (CS-003 §7.1 step 8).
5. CAM stock is the plan's Stock STL (STL S1, STL S2 and so on, one per section of a split stack) or the Fusion add-in's blank bodies, so the program and the glued block agree.

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.text:
1. Sheet stock and flat boards: place on the spoilboard, open the zones under the part, keep unused zones closed for suction where it counts. No tape, no nails.
2. Tall glued mold stacks with small footprints are the case to think about: holding force scales with footprint area, and a 6″ stack on a small base sees real side loads. Do a firm hand-push test before running; if it moves at all, add mechanical fixing (screws through waste margin into the spoilboard, or cleats) and note it in the CAM so nothing cuts there.
3. Porous/already-sealed surfaces hold differently. When in doubt, test-push and ask Larry.

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.section: 7.4 Zeroing and tooling: where SN5 lost parts
sections.text:
1. Zero Z once per setup, from the top of the stock, at the highest point of the finished stack. Never the bed. (The Feb 2026 "it plunged into the part" incidents were zeroing mistakes on the old machine; the rule carries over.) Each section of a split stack is its own setup, with its own stock STL and its own zero.
2. Tool changes are the ATC's job, not yours. The machine measures each tool's length and applies offsets from the tool table: there's no manual re-zero between tools. What that means for you:
 - Build CAM against the current FEB ShopSabre tool library (posted in #composites 2026-09-16; the older library is deprecated). A tool table that does not match the rack does the same thing a bad zero does, just faster.
 - If anyone has manually swapped a bit in a rack position, the tool must be re-measured before your program trusts it. When in doubt, run the tool-measure cycle; it costs a minute.
3. Verify X/Y zero against the stock corner and the CAM origin before starting.
4. Deep cuts: split toolpaths into depth stages rather than one full-depth pass.
5. Watch the first minutes of every program, hand near the stop.
6. Set CAM feeds for the highest board grade in the stack: the mold's Highest density cut once its boards are marked cut, or the top of its planned density range before then (CS-003 §5). The cut list prints it as "Machine at the N lb/ft³ feed." and the layer sheets repeat it (`app/stock.js`, `app/drawings.js`).

> Machine doing anything unexpected: stop first, figure it out second. A scrapped hour is cheaper than a scrapped mold stack.

![Z-zero, right and wrong. Left: touched off once per setup at the highest point of the stock. Right: zeroed at the bed, where any error in assumed stack height is a plunge into the part.](figures/cs005-zzero.v2.png)

![Feed rate for a mixed-grade stack: a mold glued from 30 and 45 lb/ft³ boards is machined at the 45 lb feed, because the densest board cut sets the feed for every setup.](figures/cs005-feed-density.v2.png)

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.section: 7.5 During the run, engraving the ID and cleanup
sections.text:
1. Stay with the machine; dust management per RFS rules.
2. Record actual machining time in the work order's Machine mold step note (this is how next season's estimates get good).
3. Check scribes/surfaces before releasing the vacuum; rework is easiest while the part is still located.
4. Engrave the mold ID on the back face before releasing the vacuum: 6 mm cap height, 1.0 mm deep, single-line font, 3.175 mm ball or 90° V-bit. The machine is set up and the part is fixtured, so it costs about 90 seconds.
5. Clean up, hand the room back better than you found it. The RFS relationship is our machining capacity.
6. Set the mold's stage to Machined and its Home location in the app. Then clean and seal per CS-004.

> The engraving is the record of record (CS-001 §7.4). It survives IPA, acetone, four coats of wax, PVA, sanding, the printed label falling off, and the label printer being broken. Every other way a mold is identified is a convenience wrapped around this one, which is why it is cut while the setup still exists rather than "later".

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.text: The work order's Machine mold step note (Glue and machine mold on a wet-layup run): operator, date, slot, estimate vs actual, tool list, incidents. The app holds the step until it has a note, and suggests a photo (`app/workorders.js`). A lead can sign without it (Sign without it), and the reason goes in the work order's event log. The mold record: stage Machined and Home location (§7.5 step 6). Actual times feed the capacity model. ~2 molds/week was SN5 reality on a worse machine; find out what this one actually does instead of assuming.

sections.title: CS-005 CNC Machining of Tooling Board (ShopSabre)
sections.section: Appendix: the Shopbot era (why this doc exists)
sections.text: Jacobs Shopbot: per-person daily slots, ShopbotBot morning scramble, 3-reservation caps, trading slots with other teams, a ~3″ cut depth that forced tall molds to be sectioned and re-glued, manual tool changes with a re-zero every time, and tape/nail workholding (tape thickness literally showed up as Z error across a sheet). We out-demanded the system, block-booked through multiple members, and on 2026-02-23 Jacobs staff formally objected. The ShopSabre fixes the access problem and most of the setup failure modes: vacuum table kills the tape-Z-error problem, the ATC kills the forgot-to-re-zero problem, 6″ of cut depth kills most mold sectioning. It does not fix physics, though; one machine, bursty demand. The habit that transfers is forward capacity planning: estimates on WOs, booking at CAM start, machine load in the weekly summary.

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text: Infusion is our main process for big parts, and in SN5 it ran without acceptance criteria: no numeric leak-down limit ("air started leaking in toward the end, hopefully it will turn out okay", #composites, 2026-05-01), an inherited guide asking people to find a physically impossible "30 psi" of vacuum, and no resin trap mentioned anywhere between bag and pump. This doc gives the numbers.

sections.text: Resin infusion of CF/glass laminates on sealed tooling-board molds (CS-004) or flat glass/table plates, using the team's IN2/AT30 system. Wet layup: CS-007.

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text:
- **inHg**: inches of mercury, what the team's gauges read for vacuum. Full vacuum at sea level ≈ 29.9 inHg; nothing reads "30 psi of vacuum", since atmospheric pressure is only ~14.7 psi. The old guide's "30 psi" figure was a gauge-scale mix-up; if a gauge shows psi, it is reading something else.
- **Drop test / leak-down**: isolating the bag from the pump and watching the gauge to quantify leaks before committing resin.
- **Resin trap / catch pot**: sealed container between bag outlet and pump that catches over-pulled resin. Without it, the first overlong pull kills the vacuum pump.
- **Pleats**: folds built into the bag with tacky tape so film can reach into corners without bridging or tearing.
- **Race-tracking**: resin finding a fast path (usually along edges) and reaching the outlet before wetting the middle.

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text:
Per R2 (§2 of each SDS): IN2 resin causes skin irritation, serious eye irritation and allergic skin reactions, and may damage fertility (H315, H319, H317, H360F). AT30 hardener, SLOW and FAST, is corrosive: it causes severe skin burns and serious eye damage (H314, H318), causes allergic skin reactions (H317) and is harmful if swallowed (H302). The AT30 FAST SDS adds possible organ damage through prolonged or repeated exposure (H373) and corrosive to the respiratory tract (EUH071).

- **Gloves:** nitrile at all times once resin is out; change after any contamination.
- **Eyes:** safety glasses with side shields (EN 166) whenever resin or hardener is open (R2 §8.2).
- **Respirator:** in a closed room or a long session, wear the team respirator with the stocked A + P100 cartridges (CS-011 §5; CS-008 §6). You should use ABEK cartridges (EN 14387) instead (R2, AT30 SLOW and FAST §8.2); they are on the purchase list.
- **Ventilation:** mix and infuse in the ventilated shop area (R2 §8.2 asks for effective ventilation in all processing areas); sensitization is cumulative.
- **Fertility:** IN2 may damage fertility (H360F). Anyone who is pregnant, trying to conceive or concerned should get medical advice before handling it (R2: P201, P308 + P313), and may ask a lead for other work on an infusion night without saying why.
- **Airtac 2 (R5):** extremely flammable aerosol: no sparks/heat, use in ventilated space, short bursts.
- **Exotherm:** a full mixed pot of IN2 left standing will overheat (CS-008 rules apply: batch sizing, transfer promptly, hot cup → outside on concrete).
- **Sharp spiral-wrap ends:** cut ends pierce gloves and bags alike; tape them.

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text:
1. Stack frozen and printed on the WO (CS-002 §7.2); mold sealed + released per CS-004 with quality checks passed.
2. Materials staged: resin on hand ≥ (dry fiber mass × 0.65) × 1.3 (same formula as the mix math in 7.5, rounded up since infusion consumes mesh/line resin too), all consumables cut before any resin is mixed.
3. Two people minimum for any part bigger than a coupon; one experienced with infusion (unchanged team rule, R7). In the app, the steps "Dry stack and bag", "Drop test, 1 inHg or less over 10 min" and "Infuse" are signed only by someone with Resin infusion training. Anyone without that training cannot sign them; only a lead can sign without it, and the reason goes in the work order's event log.

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text:
1. Wipe the workspace with IPA. Dust the released mold with a clean, dry microfiber only: no IPA, water or solvent on wax or PVA (Partall Film #10 is a water- and alcohol-based PVA, CS-004 R3). Cut cloth per the WO ply table; weigh and record total dry fiber mass on the WO.
2. Lay plies per the WO, tacking with Airtac 2 only where a ply needs holding: hold the can at least 30 cm (12 in) from the surface, mist lightly, and wait 10 s before placing the ply (R5). Heavy spray inhibits infusion.
3. Peel ply over the full laminate + flange edges; flow mesh over the entire part **stopping 30–50 mm short of the outlet side** (team rule; R8 describes the break near the outlet but gives no distance). The mesh break slows resin at the end and reduces race-tracking through the exit.
4. Place spiral-wrap feed line along the inlet side on the flange (not on part surface unless the WO says so; print-through), and the outlet spiral toward the catch pot. **Max resin travel distance inlet→outlet ≈ 0.5 m** (R8, rule of thumb; it varies with resin and part shape); larger parts need multiple feeds planned on the WO.

[PHOTO: dry stack with mesh break visible near outlet spiral]

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text:
1. Tacky tape around the full perimeter on the outer edge of the flange, outboard of everything going in the bag (spirals, peel ply, mesh), with at least ½ inch between them and the tape so nothing overlaps it (R7). Keep the backing on until final placement.
2. Cut VB160 oversized; add a pleat at every corner and every 300–400 mm of perimeter on curved molds (team rule).
3. Fit through-bag connectors: outlet line → **resin trap → pump** (never bag → pump directly); inlet line → clamped shut.

![The full loop in section, pot to pump. The flow mesh stops 30–50 mm short of the outlet, the trap sits between bag and pump, and resin travel inlet to outlet stays at or under 0.5 m.](figures/cs006-infusion.v2.png)

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.section: 7.4 Pull vacuum and drop test: the blocker
sections.text:
1. Pull vacuum. Target on the team gauge: **≥27 inHg** (team acceptance criterion, set in Rev A; full vacuum is ~29.9 inHg at sea level; RFS altitude is negligible). If the gauge won't pass 25 inHg, hunt leaks now: press tacky tape seams, listen, re-seat pleats and connector bases.
2. **Drop test: close the valve to isolate the pump. The bag must lose ≤1 inHg over 10 minutes** (team acceptance criterion, set in Rev A). The gauge must be on the bag side of the closed valve (§5). Write the start and end readings in the note on the work order's "Drop test, 1 inHg or less over 10 min" step; it will not take a member's signature without the note, and "Infuse" cannot be signed until it is. A lead can sign without it (Sign without it), and the reason goes in the work order's event log.
3. Fail → keep hunting (seams, pleat folds, connector bases, spiral ends piercing the bag) and re-test. **Do not mix resin until the drop test passes.** This number is the difference between this standard and SN5's "hopefully it will turn out okay".
4. Pass → open the valve again and check the gauge climbs back to 27 inHg before you open the inlet (§7.5 step 4). A closed valve left shut bleeds the bag down through the cure.

> The drop test is cheap. A dry patch in a cured undertray panel is not. No pass, no resin, even at 11 pm with people waiting.

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text:
1. Resin mass math: **mix ≈ (dry fiber mass × 0.65) × 1.2–1.3** (team factors; tune them from WO records). The 0.65 factor covers the laminate (aiming ~60:40 fiber:resin by weight); the 1.2–1.3 multiplier covers mesh/line losses. Round up; starving the infusion mid-pull is unrecoverable, and leftover mixed resin is a known cost (record actual used vs mixed on the WO to tune this). On a long infusion you may mix the total as two or more smaller batches and top up the pot as it draws down, keeping the inlet submerged (R1).
2. Mix IN2:AT30 **100:30 by weight** (R1) per CS-008 (double-pot, ≥2 min). SLOW hardener default: plan on 80–100 min pot life (the TDS text, no temperature given; its table says 120–150 min at 25 °C) (R1).
3. Brace the resin cup; submerge the inlet line end fully (a slurping inlet injects the bubbles you just vacuumed out).
4. With ≥27 inHg confirmed, open the inlet clamp slowly. Watch the flow front: even progress, no race-tracking. Typical infusion time: about 20–30 min on a larger piece, sometimes longer (R7); record yours on the WO.
5. When resin reaches the outlet spiral and the laminate is fully dark/wet: clamp the inlet. Leave the pump running through gel (SN5 practice; the "no 24/7 vacuum" optimization was never validated, revisit only with a deliberate test).
6. Record on the WO: times (mix, open, full-wet, clamp), resin mixed vs used, gauge readings, anomalies with photos. When you sign "Infuse", the app asks for the cure record: set Resin mixed to IN2 + AT30 SLOW (or IN2 + AT30 FAST), set Finished on and at to the time you clamped the inlet, and fill in "Shop temperature, °C (optional)". That time starts the hold on "Cure and demould".

[PHOTO: flow front mid-infusion, even progress across the part]

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text:
1. Do not demould before the FEB hold: 48 h for SLOW, 24 h for FAST, counted from the time you clamped the inlet (team hold, CS-008 §5.1). The work order's "Cure and demould" step stays locked until the hold passes; only a lead can override it, with a written reason. The datasheet demould figure is 18–24 h SLOW and 6–8 h FAST at 25 °C (R1). A colder shop runs longer than either; gel ≠ cured.
2. Full mechanical properties take ≥14 days (R1); schedule trimming freely, but no structural/fit loading before then where avoidable.
3. Demould, label part per CS-001, photograph, weigh, record in WO qualityChecks; hand to CS-009 for trim.
4. On the Molds tab, open the mold, add 1 to Parts pulled and set Stage back to Sealed: the PVA came off with the part (CS-004 R3). It goes back to Ready for layup only after the next release (CS-004 §7.4 step 4, then §7.5 step 5).

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text:
| Symptom | Likely cause | Do |
|---|---|---|
| Gauge won't reach 25 inHg (bag leak) | Perimeter leak, connector base, pleat fold | Press seams, re-seat. Soapy water only on hose fittings and connectors outside the bag, never on bag film, pleats or tape seams over a dry stack; find those by pressing and listening |
| Passes to 27 then creeps down | Micro-leak: spiral end or bag puncture | Patch with tacky tape square; re-drop-test |
| Leak you cannot find | Air drawn in through the mold itself (unsealed back or sides, cracks), or a sharp mold edge or mesh corner piercing the bag | Sand or radius sharp mold edges, or edge them with breather; chamfer or tape down mesh corners; check whether the mold's back and sides were sealed; sealing them is shop practice (Larry, #composites 2026-04-03), and CS-004 does not yet require it |
| Resin racing along one edge | Race-tracking channel at the flange | Clamp inlet briefly; rely on mesh break; note for next mold (tape a dam) |
| Dry patch far from inlet | Mesh didn't cover; distance >0.5 m | If still wet: call the experienced infuser (§7.1 step 3) about an emergency second feed; do not pierce the bag yourself. [NICK TO CONFIRM: how the team adds a second feed through a bag under vacuum.] Cured: record as defect, assess vs qualityChecks |
| White/foamy resin at inlet | Bubbles from slurping cup | Re-submerge line; bubbles usually trap in mesh, note location |
| Bubbles under a sound bag | Air drawn in during the pull | If the bag still holds, flush more resin through before clamping the inlet (shop practice, Larry, #composites 2026-04-03) |
| Resin in the trap filling fast | Over-pull past full wet | Clamp inlet earlier next time; trap is doing its job; empty before it nears the pump port |

sections.title: CS-006 Resin Infusion
sections.text:
Degassing is an optional step. The team degasses IN2 sometimes; the IN2 datasheet does not call for it (R1). Degas when the part shows its surface (a visible cosmetic face), when an earlier part from the same mold came out with pinholes or bubbles, or when the mix was stirred hard enough to look cloudy.

How: mix and double-pot first (CS-008 §7 step 3), then put the mixed cup in the degassing chamber and pull vacuum until the foam rises and collapses, then infuse straight away. [NICK TO CONFIRM: which chamber, what vacuum level and how long under the bell.]

What to watch:

- The foam rises several times the resin's height before it collapses. Leave headroom in the cup, or it boils over into the chamber.
- Time under the bell comes out of the pot life (80-100 min planned for SLOW, 9-14 min for FAST, R1). A FAST mix can spend most of its pot life under the bell, so check the clock before you start.
- A warm cup (exotherm starting) means the pot life is nearly spent. Do not infuse it; follow CS-008 for a hot cup.

Whether or not you degas, these steps keep air out of the laminate:

1. Mix and double-pot per CS-008 §7 step 3 without whipping air into the cup.
2. Keep the inlet line fully submerged in the cup for the whole infusion (§7.5 step 3).
3. Hold at least 27 inHg before the inlet opens (§7.4 step 1, §7.5 step 4).
4. Pass the drop test, 1 inHg or less over 10 min, before any resin is mixed (§7.4 step 2).
5. If bubbles show at the flow front or in the cured part, note where on the work order (§7.5 step 6), and whether the resin was degassed.

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text: Wet layup is our second core process (seat, flat panels, foam-wrapped wing elements). In SN5 the knowledge was verbal plus one Slack SOP; this doc writes it down with the numbers attached.

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
Hand lamination with West System 105 (with 206, 205 or 209 hardener), vacuum-bagged, on molds (CS-004-prepped), flat plates, and foam cores (foam-wrapped wing elements). Infusion: CS-006.

Honeycomb (Nomex) cores and inserts: the skins follow this standard. Core-specific rules (core prep, insert fit, crush limits for honeycomb) are not written yet; cores are a candidate standard in CS-INDEX.

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
- **Wet-out**: cloth fully saturated by resin: uniform sheen, weave still visible. Swimming in resin is past wet-out, not better.
- **Breather**: lofted bleed cloth between peel ply and bag. It gives air a path to the vacuum port and absorbs excess resin. It is kept clear of part edges it could bond to; resin that wicks into breather at an edge glues it on.
- **Bridging**: bag film spanning a corner instead of following it. Under vacuum a bridge either punctures or leaves a resin-rich void at the corner. Pleats exist to prevent it.
- **60:40**: target cured fiber:resin ratio **by weight**. The mix factor in §7.2 deliberately overshoots it; squeegee and breather carry the excess out.

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text: West 105 + 206 (default), 205 (small parts) or 209 (hot days and large layups; needs the shop at 70 °F / 21 °C or warmer, R6), calibrated pumps (5:1 by volume for 206 and 205, R1, R2; 3:1 by volume for 209, a different pump head, R6) or scale (weight ratios: 5.36:1 for 206, R1; 5.19:1 for 205, R2; 3.68:1 for 209, R6), brushes/rollers/squeegees, peel ply, breather, VB160, tacky tape, vacuum pump + trap + gauge, and a shut-off valve between trap and pump with the gauge on the trap or bag side of it, never on the pump (CS-006 §5).

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
The West SDSs (R7) classify the hardeners as worse than the resin. 205, 206 and 209 are each harmful if swallowed (H302), cause severe skin burns and eye damage (H314, H318) and may cause an allergic skin reaction (H317); 205 is also harmful in contact with skin (H312); 206 and 209 may also irritate the lungs (H335), 205 and 209 may damage organs through repeated exposure (H373), and 205 is suspected of causing genetic defects (H341). 105 resin irritates skin and eyes (H315, H319) and may cause an allergic skin reaction (H317). Treat 105 and its hardeners as CS-008 §6 says for every resin system.

Team rules: nitrile gloves (sensitizer; same warning as CS-004 §6), safety glasses with side shields whenever resin or hardener is open (R7 §8; CS-008 §6), ventilation, no solvent on skin; exotherm rules per CS-008 (105/205 in a pot gets hot fast). Respirator with A-filter for large overhead/enclosed laminating.

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
1. Stack frozen and printed on the WO (CS-002 §7.2). Mold sealed and released per CS-004 with its quality checks passed, or plate waxed, or foam core shaped and dry-fitted.
2. Cloth cut per the WO ply table; total dry fiber mass weighed and recorded on the WO.
3. All consumables (peel ply, breather, bag, tacky tape) cut to size before any resin is mixed. Pot life spent hunting scissors is pot life lost.
4. Check the shop temperature against the hardener's minimum before mixing: 206 needs 60 °F (16 °C), 205 needs 40 °F (4 °C), 209 needs 70 °F (21 °C) (datasheet minimums, R1, R2, R6). Below it, pick a hardener whose minimum the shop meets, or wait.

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
1. Mix mass ≈ **dry fiber mass × 0.9** (team factor). That is deliberately more than the 60:40 cured target implies: the squeegee and the breather take the excess out, and the *cured part* lands near 60:40. Record mixed and final masses on the WO to tune this factor.
2. Mix per CS-008 discipline. With the calibrated pumps, **5:1 by volume, one FULL stroke of each pump per shot, never partial strokes** (R1). By scale: 5.36:1 for 206, 5.19:1 for 205 (CS-008 §5). 209 uses the 3:1 pumps, not the 5:1 pumps: check the pump head before the first stroke. By scale, 209 is 3.68:1 (R6).
3. Pot life budget, 206 at 72 °F: **20–25 min per 100 g pot** (R1). 205: 9–12 min per 100 g at 72 °F (R2). 209: 40–50 min per 100 g at 72 °F (R6). Bigger jobs mix several small pots rather than one large one; a pot that warms is a pot that is about to gel (CS-008 §6).

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
1. Wet out ply-by-ply per the WO ply table: resin on, then squeegee each ply until **shiny-wet with the weave visible**, not swimming. Chase dry (white) patches before the next ply goes on; you will not see them again.
2. Check each ply against the run's stack (Stack & BOM) as it goes on. Edit any change, a substitution or an extra ply, into the run's stack and write the reason in that ply's Notes (CS-002 §7.4). A pen tick on a printed traveler is allowed as well.

[PHOTO: correctly wetted ply: uniform sheen, weave visible, no pooling]

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
1. Peel ply over the full laminate, past its edges.
2. Breather over the peel ply, held back from every part edge it could bond to (Figure 1).
3. Bag with VB160 and tacky tape, pleats at corners and every 300–400 mm of curved perimeter; CS-006 §7.3 rules apply, including the trap between bag and pump.
4. Where the WO says so, you may replace the peel ply with a release film (A4000R) or a mylar sheet, or add a caul plate over the peel ply. These are still under test (2026-09). Write which one you used in the WO and photograph the finished surface.

![The wet-layup bag in section. The breather covers the peel ply but stops short of every part edge; resin that wicks into breather at an edge bonds it to the part.](figures/cs007-bag-stack.v2.png)

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
1. Pull to **≥25 inHg** (team acceptance criterion).
2. Drop test before walking away: isolate the pump; the bag shall lose **≤2 inHg over 10 minutes** (team acceptance criterion). The gauge must be on the bag side of the closed valve (CS-006 §5). Write the start and end readings in the note on the "Wet layup and bag" step ("Wet layup over core" on a Foam wrapped run). Leak hunting per CS-006 §7.7.
3. On light foam cores, watch for vacuum crush: if the core dents, reduce vacuum and record the level that held on the WO, per part, so the next build starts from a number.
4. After the drop test passes, open the valve again and check the gauge climbs back to 25 inHg before you walk away. A valve left shut bleeds the bag down overnight.

The Mold wet lay and Foam wrapped techniques have no drop-test step, so the app does not block on this test. The cure hold reads only the step directly before it, so a drop-test step placed between "Wet layup and bag" and "Cure and demould" (or "Cure") would switch the hold off. Until the app changes, the drop test is recorded in the "Wet layup and bag" note.

[PHOTO: bagged wet layup under vacuum, pleats visible, gauge in frame]

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
1. Leave bagged under vacuum overnight minimum. 206 reaches thin-film solid in **10–15 h at 72 °F** (R1); a cold shop runs longer. Before you leave, record the buy-off:

 - Sign "Wet layup and bag" ("Wet layup over core" on a Foam wrapped run); signing needs Wet layup training in the app.
 - Under "Resin mixed", pick West 105 + 206 slow, West 105 + 205 fast or West 105 + 209 extra slow, whichever you mixed.
 - Set "Finished on" and "at" to when you finished bagging.
 - Fill in "Shop temperature, °C (optional)". That starts the FEB hold.
2. Demold no earlier than the FEB hold: 24 h for 206 and 205, 36 h for 209 (team holds, CS-008 §5; the datasheet thin-film cure is 10–15 h, 6–8 h and 20–24 h at 72 °F, R1, R2, R6). "Cure and demould" ("Cure" on Foam wrapped) stays locked until the hold is up. Only a lead can sign it early, and the app makes them write why.
3. Record times and masses on the WO; label the part per CS-001; hand to CS-009 for trim.
4. On the Molds tab, open the mold, add 1 to Parts pulled and set Stage back to Sealed: the PVA came off with the part (CS-004 R3). It goes back to Ready for layup only after the next release (CS-004 §7.4 step 4, then §7.5 step 5). Not for a foam core or a plate.

sections.title: CS-007 Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging
sections.text:
The same flow over a shaped foam core instead of a mold: wet plies wrap the core, then peel ply, breather, bag. The §7.5 crush rule is the one that bites here; everything else is unchanged.

In the app this is the Foam wrapped technique. Its steps are "Stack frozen", "Shape foam core" (needs Foam core training), "Wet layup over core" (needs Wet layup training; signing it starts the cure hold, §7.6 step 1), "Cure" (the hold) and "Trim and finish".

| Wet-out | No white/dry weave visible | Visual per ply | WO |

sections.title: CS-008 Resins, Mixing & Cure Schedules
sections.text:
- **Pot life**: usable time in the mixing pot, at the mass and temperature the TDS states it for. Bigger batch or warmer shop means shorter; the quoted figure is the ceiling, not a promise.
- **Gel**: the resin no longer flows. Gel is not cure: a gelled part pried off a mold drags resin with it.
- **Demould**: the earliest the part can leave the mold without damage. Two columns in §5: the datasheet cure figure and the FEB hold that governs (§5.1).
- **Full cure**: full mechanical properties. Weeks, not hours, for every system we stock; no structural or fit loading before then where avoidable.
- **Exotherm**: the cure reaction's own heat. Mass concentrated in a cup accelerates it; the runaway case is §6's hot-cup rule.

sections.title: CS-008 Resins, Mixing & Cure Schedules
sections.section: 5.1 The two demould columns, and which one is the rule (1/2)
sections.text:
**Datasheet cure figure** is what the manufacturer publishes, at the temperature
they publish it at: a demould time for IN2, a thin-film cure for West, an
initial cure for XCR. Every figure is quoted from a TDS in `03 Datasheets/`.

**FEB hold** is what this team waits, and it is the one that governs. It is
longer than the datasheet in every row, on purpose, and it is a team decision
rather than a manufacturer claim, so it is never presented as one. Signed off
by Simon Starbuck, 2026-08-01.

The holds are shift boundaries, not multiples of the datasheet: 24 h means "come
back tomorrow" and 48 h means "come back the day after tomorrow" (after the
weekend, for a Friday infusion). A hold that expires
at 3 am helps nobody, because nobody is at RFS at 3 am. That is why the ratios
against the datasheet look uneven (1.3× for XCR, 3× for the FAST systems); they
were never derived from it.

Both FAST systems hold 24 h, so buying FAST hardener to turn two infusions
round in one day does not work under this rule. That is deliberate: we have no
record of a part ruined by waiting and several of work being rushed. But it is
the line to revisit if the trade stops being worth it.

A cold shop is not covered by these numbers. Every figure assumes the
reference temperature in its row. We cure ambient with no oven, and RFS in
January is not 25 °C. Log the temperature per §7 step 5 and fingernail-test the
flange (§8) rather than trusting the clock. When the recorded shop temperature
is below the datasheet's reference (25 °C for IN2, 22 °C for West, 20 °C for
XCR, from `resins.js`), the app warns "Colder than this number assumes, so it
will run long. Test the flange, not the clock." It leaves the hold unchanged.

![Datasheet cure figure (thin solid bar) against the FEB hold that governs (hollow bar), per system, on one time axis. The holds land on shift boundaries, which is why both FAST systems still hold 24 h.](figures/cs008-holds.v2.png)

sections.title: CS-008 Resins, Mixing & Cure Schedules
sections.section: 5.1 The two demould columns, and which one is the rule (2/2)
sections.text:
**What the app enforces.** Signing the step that starts a cure ("Infuse", "Wet
layup and bag", "Wet layup over core") opens a buy-off that asks for "Resin
mixed", "Finished on" and "at", and "Shop temperature, °C (optional)". The next
step ("Cure and demould", or "Cure" on a Foam wrapped run) stays locked until
the FEB hold for that resin has run from the finish time. A member who tries to
sign it early is turned away. A lead may sign it early through "Demould early?",
which asks "Why are you demoulding early?" and writes the reason, the lead's
name and how many hours short it was to the work order's event log.

**What the app does not lock.** Mold sealing with XCR: no work-order step starts
an XCR cure, so its 12 h hold is watched by hand (CS-004 §7.3). Any cure
recorded as "Something else / not recorded": no resin means no hold. Retro
work orders, the records of SN5 runs, enforce nothing.

**Changing a hold.** The §5 table is the code table in
`06 Composites App/app/resins.js` at this revision, signed off 2026-08-01. The
live value is the app's. A lead may change a hold from the app, from a work
order whose hold for that resin is currently running: on the held step, press
"why N h?" to open "Why N hours?", press "Change this hold…", enter
"FEB hold (hours)", pick who signed it off and the date under "Signed off by",
and press "Save". The app refuses a hold below the datasheet figure and a hold
nobody signed off, and the change reaches every work order at once. "Revert to
the code table" in the same window undoes it. "Why N hours?" always shows the
hold in force and who signed it, and says when a lead set it from the app. A
lead who changes a hold shall open a revision of this standard within two weeks,
so the §5 table and the app agree again (CS-000 §2). A code-table hold shorter
than its datasheet figure fails the app's tests.

sections.title: CS-008 Resins, Mixing & Cure Schedules
sections.section: 6. Safety: exotherm and sensitization (applies to every system) (2/2)
sections.text:
- Every resin and hardener here can make you allergic through the skin (H317). None is classified as a respiratory sensitizer (no SDS on file carries H334), but the XCR resin SDS §11.1 says it may be a respiratory tract sensitiser, so treat its vapour with the respirator rule below. Every hardener burns skin and can blind (H314, H318). PPE: nitrile gloves; safety glasses with side shields (EN 166); ventilation; wash skin with soap, not solvent.
- **Respirator:** for long or enclosed sessions, wear the team respirator with the stocked A + P100 cartridges (CS-011 §5); the A filter covers XCR, whose SDS asks for A1 (XCR SDS §8.2). For AT30 work you should use ABEK cartridges instead (AT30 SDS §8.2).
- **Goggles:** you should wear EN 166 goggles with side protection while pouring and mixing XCR (XCR SDS §8.2); until they are bought, safety glasses with side shields. ABEK cartridges and the goggles are on the purchase list.
- Resin or hardener in an eye: rinse with plenty of water, under the eyelids too, for at least 15 minutes, then get medical attention (R4: IN2 and AT30 SDS §4; West 205 SDS §4).
- **Exotherm rules:** mix the smallest batch that does the job; pour out of the pot promptly (mass concentrated in a cup accelerates); a warm cup = use immediately or spread thin; a hot/smoking cup = carry outside onto concrete and leave it. Do not bin, do not water-dilute indoors. Nothing goes in the trash until fully cured and cool.
- Never mix off-ratio to "speed up" or "slow down" cure; off-ratio = uncured sticky part. For IN2 you may blend AT30 FAST and SLOW instead, keeping the total at 100:30 by weight (R1). For West, no datasheet on file covers blending 205 and 206: do not blend them until one does.

sections.title: CS-008 Resins, Mixing & Cure Schedules
sections.text:
1. Pick the system from §5 by process standard, with pot life to spare for the job.

 Before you mix, you should check the expiry: the EXP date on the jug's label, or the Expires date on its lot page. Past it, ask a lead before it goes on a part.

 ⚠ 209 uses 3:1 pumps, not the 5:1 pumps used by 205/206. Check the pump head before stroking; this is the classic wrong-ratio trap.
2. Weigh (scale, 1 g) or pump (West, full strokes only); record masses on the WO.
3. Mix ≥2 min scraping walls/base (team margin over the IN2 TDS's 1 min; the XCR TDS asks for "a couple of minutes"); double-pot (transfer + remix, fresh stick) for anything going on a part surface.
4. Forged CF mix math (R5): finished part mass ≈ cavity volume × 1.4 g/cc; fiber mass = 60% of that (pre-weigh it); resin to mix ≈ fiber mass × 1.25 (the excess squeezes out). Starving the mix made the first part brittle (failed bend test); don't eyeball it.
5. Cure at ≥20 °C wherever possible; log ambient temp on the WO when it isn't (cold cures run long; see each TDS).
6. Do not demould before the FEB hold in §5 has elapsed, counted from the end of the layup or infusion. The work order enforces this and records the resin, the finish time and the shop temperature; it is a lead call to go early, and the reason is logged.

 Gel is not cure: fingernail-test the flange (§8) before you trust either the clock or the feel of the part.

 When you sign the layup or infusion, pick the resin you actually mixed under "Resin mixed". Choose "Something else / not recorded" only for a resin not in §5; then write the resin in the step note, and its demould time is a lead's call.
7. Leftovers: spread thin on scrap or leave outside to cure; label per CS-001.
8. Cloudy or crystallized 105 after a cold spell: warm it to 125 °F and stir until clear before it goes in the pump (R3).
9. After a long gap between uses, mix a small test batch to check the West pumps meter correctly and the batch cures, before a part depends on them (R3).

sections.title: CS-009 Trimming, Sanding & Finishing
sections.text:
- **Sacrificial ply**: the 88 spread-tow outer layer specified in the stack (CS-002 §7.1 step 3) to absorb sanding. It is the sanding budget; structural plies are not.
- **Trim line**: the part's cut boundary, transferred from the mold's scribe lines at demold.
- **Keying**: abrading a bond face so adhesive has something to grip. The team uses 120 grit; the DP420 TDS asks only for clean, fine-grit abrasive (R1).
- **Open time**: the longest a joint may wait after adhesive goes on a face before it is closed and fixed. 20 min for DP420 (R1).
- **Handling strength**: the point where a bonded joint can be unclamped and moved, not loaded. 2.5 h at 23 °C (73 °F) for DP420 (R1).
- **Load-carrying bond**: any bond that carries load on the car: an insert, a rod end, a mount, a bracket.

sections.text:
- **CF dust is the team's worst routine exposure.** Run the dust extractor at the cut for any cutting or sanding of cured laminate, and wear the PPE in the table below for the task. The shop stocks A + P100 cartridges (`inventory.js` restock table); 3M 60921 is the OV/P100 cartridge on file (R9) | Shall: nitrile gloves (cut CF edges splinter). Long sleeves | Shall: safety glasses with side shields | Team rule (SN5); R9 |

sections.title: CS-009 Trimming, Sanding & Finishing
sections.text:
- **Supervision rule (set in SN5; the Composites Lead may change it): no cutting cured carbon without a second trained person present.** Trained means the person holds the Trimming and finishing training in the app. The Composites Lead adds that training in People → Catalog ("Add a training", CS standard CS-009) and may gate the "Trim and finish" step on it from Reports → Layup techniques → Edit steps ("Training to sign").
- Waterjet per Jacobs shop rules.
- **Clear coat (LiME LiNE UC4:1):** the Part A SDS (R6) classes it as a highly flammable liquid and vapor (H225) that may cause an allergic skin reaction (H317), causes serious eye irritation (H319) and may cause drowsiness or dizziness (H336). It says to use it only outdoors or in a well-ventilated area and to wear protective gloves, protective clothing, and eye and face protection. Part B, the activator, is an isocyanate (`03 Datasheets/INDEX.md`, LiME LiNE row) and its SDS is not on file. Nobody shall open, mix or apply Part B until its SDS, or the hazard text from the can's label, is in `03 Datasheets/` and this section quotes its PPE.

sections.title: CS-009 Trimming, Sanding & Finishing
sections.text:
1. Trim no earlier than the FEB hold for the resin system (CS-008 §5). On the run, "Trim and finish" comes after "Cure and demould" ("Cure" on a Foam wrapped run), the step that carries that hold.
2. Mark the cut from the scribe-transferred trim line. Tape the cut path: the tape controls chips and shows the line under dust.
3. Cut with the extractor running and a second trained person present (§6). Cut outside the line and sand to it; a Dremel does not steer well enough to cut on it.

sections.title: CS-009 Trimming, Sanding & Finishing
sections.text:
1. Read the run's stack before sanding anything. The sanding budget is the sacrificial ply and only the sacrificial ply (Figure 1).
2. Zones under 3 plies: hand-sand only, count strokes, check often. Machine-sanding thin laminate is how the catch cans died (R2).

![Left: the sacrificial ply is the sanding budget; structural plies are not an allowance. Right: the catch-can failure, a machine sander on thin laminate at a taper, through the skin and into the substrate.](figures/cs009-sacrificial.v2.png)

3. Edges: 120 → 400 grit. Seal exposed edge fibers with a thin resin wipe where cosmetics or sealing matter; a raw CF edge wicks moisture and splinters into hands.

If structural weave shows past the plan:

4. Stop sanding.
5. Press ⚑ (Report an issue on this step) on "Trim and finish" ("Finish" on a Glass infusion run).
6. Add the spot under "Photos of the defect".
7. Leave the Disposition to the part's engineer or the Composites Lead. The run cannot complete until the issue is disposed.
sections.status: Draft, pending Lead signature (photos to add at first SN6 use)

sections.title: CS-009 Trimming, Sanding & Finishing
sections.text:
1. Put gloves on and put out ignition sources before any solvent is opened (§6, R1). Wipe both bond faces with IPA to lift oil and release agent.
2. Abrade both faces with 120 grit until the gloss is gone (team value; the TDS asks for clean, fine-grit abrasive, R1).
3. Wipe both faces again with clean IPA. On cured laminate and metal parts away from any mold, acetone may be used instead, as the TDS's own FRP test prep does (Acetone/Abrade/Acetone, R1). Never acetone on or near tooling board (CS-004 §7.1). Let the faces flash off.
4. Change into clean gloves and keep them on. Do not touch the bond faces from here.
5. Load the duo-pak cartridge in the EPX applicator, remove the cap, and dispense a little until both sides flow evenly. Then fit the mixing nozzle (R1).
6. DP420 mixes 2:1 by volume (B:A), 2:0.98 by weight; the cartridge sets the ratio (R1). Apply, then close and fix the joint within the 20 min open time (R1).
7. Clamp so squeeze-out forms a continuous fillet, and leave the clamps on until handling strength, 2.5 h at 23 °C (73 °F) (R1). That fillet is the §8 acceptance look. The TDS reports bond strength after 7 days at 23 °C; a joint that will carry load follows §7.6.

[PHOTO: DP420 bond with continuous squeeze-out fillet: the §8 acceptance look]

sections.title: CS-009 Trimming, Sanding & Finishing
sections.section: 7.4 Clear coat a part: mixing and applying LiME LiNE UC4:1
sections.text:
1. Do not open, mix or apply Part B (the activator) until its SDS or label hazard text is on file and §6 quotes its PPE.
2. Scuff the part, wipe it with IPA, and apply the part label (CS-001 §7.5). The TDS asks for a substrate free of grease, dirt and contaminants (R5).
3. Mix 4 parts UC4:1 clear with 1 part activator (R5).
4. Use the mix within its pot life, 2 h at 77 °F / 25 °C (R5).
5. Apply 2 medium wet coats, 10 to 15 min apart (R5). To recoat after 24 h, scuff first (R5).
6. Leave the coat to cure before handling: the TDS gives dust free at 30 min and sand and buff at 12 to 24 h air dry, both at 77 °F / 25 °C (R5).
7. Record the activator, the number of coats and the time in the "Trim and finish" note ("Finish" on a Glass infusion run).

sections.section: 7.5 Cutting flat panels: waterjet, ShopSabre or bandsaw
sections.text:
1. The DXF comes from the requesting subteam through the WO, never a DM (the dashboard lesson, PP-04). Confirm the revision on the WO before cutting; on a Glass infusion run this is the "Cut to DXF, confirm revision" step.
2. Pick the machine by the job and your training: the Jacobs Hall OMAX waterjet (Jacobs waterjet training; Jacobs shop rules govern it), the RFS ShopSabre (CS-005 governs it; ask RFS staff before machining G10), or the RFS composites bandsaw (RFS composites bandsaw training) (R8).
3. On the ShopSabre and the bandsaw, the §6 dust rules apply: extractor running, respirator on, second trained person present.

sections.title: CS-009 Trimming, Sanding & Finishing
sections.section: 7.6 Bonding inserts and hardware into CF tube and parts
sections.text:
1. Every load-carrying bond shall use DP420 (R7).
2. Never use 5-minute epoxy or superglue (CA) on a load-carrying joint. In September testing an undertray insert turned out to have been bonded with 5-minute epoxy (R7).
3. Prep both faces per §7.3 steps 1 to 4. On a metal insert or rod end, abrade the full bonded length, not a few file strokes.
4. Mask the threads, and dam the tube behind the insert so adhesive cannot reach the threads or run down the tube. DP420 that reached a rod-end thread locked the rod at a set length (R7).
5. Purge the cartridge until both sides flow before fitting the mixing nozzle (§7.3 step 5).
6. Hold the bondline at the gap the drawing calls for. The TDS's test bondline is 0.13 to 0.20 mm (5 to 8 mil) (R1); the team has not set its own gap.
7. Fixture or clamp the joint so it cannot move until handling strength, 2.5 h at 23 °C (73 °F) (R1).
8. Do not load the joint (mount it on the car, torque a rod end, drive) before the team hold: [lead input needed]. The TDS reports bond strength after 7 days at 23 °C (R1). In September an insert was mounted about an hour after bonding (R7). The app does not enforce this hold; the person bonding does.
9. Record in the note on the step where the bond is done ("Trim and finish"; "Finish" on a Glass infusion run; "Execute" on an Other run): adhesive and lot, prep done, time bonded, and time first loaded.

![Section through a CF tube with a bonded insert: solvent, abrade, solvent on both faces; the bondline gap (DP420 TDS test bondline 0.13 to 0.20 mm); a dam inside the tube; masked threads; no load before the team hold.](figures/cs009-insert-bond.v2.png)

sections.title: CS-010 CF Grounding & Electrical Bonding
sections.text: EV rules want conductive parts near HV/chassis grounded (our SN5 working criterion: <5 Ω to the grounding point). SN5 gave us both the success story and the cautionary tale. The diffuser (target and method written down up front, copper mesh in the stack) validated at <1 Ω continuous everywhere (2026-06-21) and drew praise from the design judges at comp. The catch can had no written criterion; its method was improvised for six months (Nov→May) and never hit target with CF wrapping, so the team gave up on CF for that geometry and pivoted to epoxy + copper paths (PP-05). WO-SN5-026 records no passing measurement after the pivot. This doc exists so we repeat the first one.

sections.title: CS-010 CF Grounding & Electrical Bonding
sections.text:
Any CF part with a grounding/bonding requirement, and any conductive-path retrofit on existing parts. The Ω target and rule interpretation come from the EV rules owner (powertrain/rules lead); this standard covers how composites *achieves and proves* the target, not what the target legally is.

Requests from other subteams (cooling, brakes, aero) arrive as a work order with the Other technique. The Ω and distance targets on them stay the rules owner's numbers.

sections.title: CS-010 CF Grounding & Electrical Bonding
sections.text:
- **Grounding point**: the fastener/tab where the part's conductive path meets chassis ground.
- **Probe pattern**: the defined set of surface points measured against the grounding point.
- **CF as conductor**: carbon laminate conducts, but through-thickness resistance through resin-rich layers is high and unpredictable; bare CF also can't be reliably terminated. Hence copper mesh.
- **Surface path**: a conductor applied to the cured part's surface: copper strip or braid bonded with epoxy, copper tape, or conductive paint.

sections.text:

sections.title: CS-010 CF Grounding & Electrical Bonding
sections.text:
Grounding verification happens on or near the car: follow EV safety rules. No probing near energized HV; HV isolation confirmed by the ESO before resistance measurements on installed parts. Bench measurements on loose parts: no special hazards beyond CS-009 dust rules if sanding contact points.

Graphite powder (§5, §7.2 step 4): wear the respirator with a P100 cartridge and nitrile gloves while weighing and mixing it. The shop stocks A + P100 cartridges and nitrile gloves (`inventory.js` restock table). No graphite SDS is on file yet. Cut copper mesh has sharp wire ends: wear gloves when cutting and placing it.

sections.title: CS-010 CF Grounding & Electrical Bonding
sections.text:
1. Before any layup work, decide whether CF with copper mesh is the right conductive path for this geometry. Write the answer and a one-line why in the note on "Stack frozen". A retrofit or a cross-team grounding job is created with the Other technique, and the answer goes in the note on "Define acceptance criterion: target and method, set before work starts", the step that blocks everything after it.
 - **Good fit:** large open laminates (diffuser, panels) where mesh lays flat in the stack and terminates at accessible flange points.
 - **Bad fit:** thin-walled, tapered, or wrapped metal substrates (the catch can: sanding punctured the can wall at the taper; through-thickness contact never stabilized). For these, use a surface path, or reconsider whether the part needs CF at all.
 - **Surface path:** copper strip or braid bonded with epoxy, copper tape, or conductive paint, applied after cure. Weigh mass as well as geometry: mesh in the stack is heavy on a large part like the undertray (R7).
2. Write the acceptance criterion before work starts: Ω target, probe pattern (grid spacing or named points), and measurement method (7.3). On the run, add a Quality row ("+ check" in edit mode) with Criterion "grounding resistance" and fill its Target when the run is created. On an Other run, write the same criterion in the note on "Define acceptance criterion: target and method, set before work starts". Six months of drift happened because none of this was written (R1).
3. A conductive path this team has not yet proven is proven on a first article by the §7.3 method before any part depends on it.

![Choosing the conductive path: mesh in the stack, a surface path, or no CF, decided by geometry, permeability in an infusion, mass, and access to the grounding point.](figures/cs010-path-decision.v2.png)

sections.title: CS-010 CF Grounding & Electrical Bonding
sections.section: 7.2 Build the path (mesh-in-stack method: the diffuser recipe)
sections.text:
1. Put copper mesh in the ply table per CS-002: mesh layer(s) positioned to be continuous from part surface zones to the grounding point(s), 25 mm minimum overlap (team value) where mesh sheets meet. Name the ply's material "copper mesh" so the stack view tags it Mesh. Only permeable mesh shall go in an infused stack: foil, solid sheet or a paint film blocks resin flow (R7).
2. Mesh must reach the grounding point as bare, terminable material: leave a mesh tail at the flange/fastener location, protected during infusion (peel-ply window or masked zone).
3. For surfaces needing exposed conductivity, an 88-gsm outer ply over mesh keeps finish while staying thin; validate on the first article that surface-to-ground still passes.
4. Graphite powder (about 5 wt% in the resin, the SN5 trial value, R3; team value) may be added as a *supplement* in zones where mesh coverage is marginal, never as the primary path (SN5 trials judged it insufficient alone, R3). If used, record wt% on the WO.
5. Infuse/laminate per CS-006/CS-007. Note on the WO where mesh actually ended up (as-built).

![The mesh-in-stack path in plan: sheets overlapping ≥25 mm, a bare terminable tail at the grounding point, and the default probe pattern (100 mm grid plus edge midpoints). Every point measures to the grounding point; every point passes or the part does not.](figures/cs010-mesh-path.v2.png)

[PHOTO: copper mesh tail at grounding point before bagging]

sections.title: CS-010 CF Grounding & Electrical Bonding
sections.text:
1. Zero the multimeter leads; record lead resistance.
2. Fasten the grounding hardware as it will fly (torqued, washers as designed); hand-held contact readings are noise.
3. Probe every point in the run's probe pattern (default: 100 mm grid over conductive zones + every edge midpoint) to the grounding point. Record each value minus lead offset as a table in the note of the measuring step ("Trim and finish" on Mold infusion, Mold wet lay and Foam wrapped runs; "Finish" on a Glass infusion run; "Verify against criterion" on an Other run). Write the worst reading as the Actual on the "grounding resistance" Quality row.
4. Pass = every point ≤ target (default <5 Ω, or the rules value on the run). Not "one good point": that question was still open in May 2026, six months in (R1). A point over target is an issue: press ⚑ (Report an issue on this step) on the measuring step, and fix it per §7.4 before it is disposed.

sections.title: CS-010 CF Grounding & Electrical Bonding
sections.text:
1. Map the failing zone; usually a mesh discontinuity or resin-isolated overlap.
2. Fixes in order of preference: expose + bond a copper strip bridge (epoxy + copper path), add an external ground tab at the failing zone, or lightly abrade to mesh at a termination point and re-terminate. Do not sand thin laminates chasing contact. That is how the catch cans died (R1).
3. Re-measure the full pattern after any fix, not just the failed point.

sections.title: CS-010 CF Grounding & Electrical Bonding
sections.text:
The run keeps: the path decision and its one-line why (the "Stack frozen" note, or the criterion step's note on an Other run), the criterion (the "grounding resistance" Quality row), the full probe-reading table (values, not "pass") in the measuring step's note, photos of mesh placement and termination, and any retrofit fixes with their ⚑ issues.

WO-SN5-006 (UT diffuser) is the reference part: target set up front, method recorded, <1 Ω at comp on 2026-06-21 (R4, R5). Its record holds that summary only, not a probe table; the first SN6 grounded part will hold the first full one. WO-SN5-026 (catch can, about 40 Ω on 2026-05-25 against <5 Ω needed) is the counter-example (R6).

sections.title: CS-011 Inventory, Storage & Transport
sections.text:
- **Min-stock**: the level that triggers a reorder, sized so the order lands before stock-out at the supplier's lead time.
- **Stock walk**: the monthly check of every shelf against its record (§7.1). The app records it per shelf as Contents last confirmed and Confirmed by.
- **Home location**: the storage record (`BIN-SN6-###`) an object belongs on. Molds and material lots carry it in their Home location field.
- **Lot**: one recorded container or roll (`FAB-SN6-###`, `RSN-SN6-###`, `CON-SN6-###`); a consumable lot is one record with a count. CS-014 owns lots.
- **Material type**: the app's name for a kind of material across every container of it, for example `IN2`, `AT30` or `WEST-105`. Restock rules and a shelf page's grouping both key on it.
- **Restock rule**: one row of the §5 table as the app holds it: Material type, minimum, unit, supplier and lead time.
- **How full**: a lot's level, Full, Half, Low or Empty. An Empty container counts as zero toward the minimum; an opened one counts as one container (`app/inventory.js`, `restockOnHand`).

sections.title: CS-011 Inventory, Storage & Transport
sections.section: 5. Minimum stock: what we never run out of (1/3)
sections.text:
These are starting values, tuned with usage data. Sizing rule (§4): min stock = (burn rate × supplier lead time) + one job's worth. Worked examples for the three items that actually stop a layup; the rest of the table starts as one-job buffers, tuned with WO usage data:

- **IN2 + AT30:** about 1.95 kg mixed per large infusion (team estimate; no logged source); at the 2-infusions/week peak that is ~4 kg/week. Easy Composites lead ≥6 weeks (CS-012) → running dry mid-season costs ~6 weeks of infusions. One unopened kit (~4 kg, team estimate) ≈ 1 peak week: it is the alarm, not the buffer. When the walk finds only the unopened kit, the order is already late, so trigger at opened kit + 1 unopened, and place the big seasonal orders per CS-012 §7.4 so the walk never trips this.
- **XCR:** ~1 kit seals 2–3 mold sections (tune from WO records); molds queue 2/week in peak → 1 kit ≈ 1 week. Same logic: 1 unopened kit minimum, ordered with every EC basket.
- **Tacky tape:** every bagged job uses 1–2 rolls of perimeter; 2 jobs/week → ~3 rolls/week; domestic lead ~1 week → 6 rolls ≈ 2 weeks of peak burn.

sections.title: CS-011 Inventory, Storage & Transport
sections.text:
The walk takes about 15 minutes (team estimate). An IA or first-year is the right owner; it is a good first responsibility.

1. The lead names the stock-walk owner at the start of the season.
2. Once a month, open Inventory → Storage map and walk each shelf: open its card, check the list against what is on the shelf, and press Confirm contents (Confirm on the map card does the same).
3. Fix what is wrong as you go: Move for something on the wrong shelf, How full on a container, and the shelf's Add here card for anything missing.
4. Open the Running out card on the storage map. If any row lacks "on order", press Add N to a purchase, pick A new purchase or an open purchase under Add to, and press Add to purchase.
5. Post the purchase request in #purchasing-slackbot the same day (CS-012 §7.1).

Between walks, open one container of a material at a time and mark an emptied container Empty rather than deleting it: the cure buy-off pre-fills the most recently opened lot, and the reorder count needs to see the empty one (CS-014 §7.8).

sections.section: 7.6 Storage temperature and shelf life (resins, hardeners and XCR)
sections.text:
Keep every resin and hardener container closed. The figures below are datasheet figures (R7), not team holds. Where each container lives is §6 and §7.3.

| Material | Store at | Shelf life | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| IN2 resin and AT30 hardener | 10–25 °C (50–77 °F), tightly sealed | 12 months when stored correctly | `03 Datasheets/EC-TDS-IN2-Infusion-Resin.pdf` |
| XCR resin and hardener | 20–25 °C (68–77 °F), tightly sealed | 12 months when stored correctly | `03 Datasheets/EC-TDS-XCR-Epoxy-Coating-Resin.pdf` |
| West System 105 with 205, 206 or 209 | Room temperature, containers closed | Usable for many years with proper storage | `03 Datasheets/west-system_slow-epoxy-hardener_206_tds.pdf`, `03 Datasheets/105_205-207-Combined.pdf`, `03 Datasheets/105-209-Epoxy-Resin-1.pdf` |

1. Do not let West 105 freeze and thaw repeatedly: it crystallizes (`03 Datasheets/west-system_slow-epoxy-hardener_206_tds.pdf`). Crystallized 105 is warmed to 125 °F and stirred before use; CS-008 §7 step 8 owns that step.
2. After long storage, check the West pumps' metering and mix a small test batch to confirm it cures (same TDS).

sections.text:

sections.title: CS-012 Purchasing & Reimbursement
sections.section: 7.1 Getting a purchase approved (before you buy)
sections.text:
Get approval before you buy anything. The bot sends each request to the approver for its amount (R1).

1. Run `/purchase` in #purchasing-slackbot with the budget reference ID (§7.2 step 4), the amount and the reason. For several items on different reference IDs, use `/bigorder`.
2. The bot routes the request by tier: under $50 to the subteam lead, $50 to $250 to the division lead, over $250 to the President or VP (R1).
3. Buy only after the bot's approval DM arrives.

The Budget tab follows the purchase on two tracks (R6). Write the bot's REQ number in the purchase's Notes.

| Track | Status | Means |
|---|---|---|
| Order status (the goods) | Submitted | Requested in the bot, not bought yet |
| Order status (the goods) | Purchased | Bought, after the approval DM |
| Order status (the goods) | Arrived | Here and received into Inventory (CS-014 §7.5 step 11). Set it by hand; receiving does not change it |
| Reimbursement (the money) | Submitted | Owed to the purchaser |
| Reimbursement (the money) | Approved | The bot's approval DM came back |
| Reimbursement (the money) | Reimbursed | Paid back |

The Budget tab counts purchases over $50 whose Reimbursement is still Submitted ("Over $50, unapproved"). A purchase under $50 still needs the subteam lead's approval; the app does not flag it.

![One purchase on two tracks: the goods and the money](figures/cs012-purchase-tracks.v2.png)

sections.text:
1. Photograph the itemized receipt, or save the PDF invoice an online order emails you. A card statement alone is not enough.

3. Amazon orders: the order must show Shipped or Delivered before submitting.
4. Pick the budget reference ID for the line the money comes from: `/reference` lists them, and composites lines start `COMP-`. Testing purchases use `TRAN-012` (Ishaan Sid, #purchasing, 2026-10-09). Use a `-000` ID only for something the budget never listed, and tell the lead, because it comes out of another line.
5. Log the purchase in the bot (§7.1) and submit it for reimbursement within one month of the purchase (R4), with `/reimburse`, the reference ID and the amount (R1). Cash, Venmo, Zelle and PayPal are not reimbursed; ask the finance lead before paying with one (R1). Gift cards: ask the finance lead first (the 2025 rules excluded them, R4).
6. Attach the receipt to the purchase in the Budget tab with + Add / scan receipt. Put the quote and order confirmation under Other files.
7. To use ✨ Fill from receipt, press Edit first; the button shows in Edit when a receipt is attached and a lead has AI features on. Check every proposed line against the receipt before you leave the page. Anything a ✨ button fills is a draft until a person checks it (CS-014 §7.4).

sections.text:
Filed here rather than left implicit: the printer is the one CS-001 §5 item the team has not bought.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Item** | A Brother QL-series label printer on the shed wifi, printing over AirPrint, plus Brother DK-2210 29 mm continuous rolls (cut at 101.6 mm) and Brother DK-1201 29 x 90 mm die-cut rolls as the fallback. These are the printer and media the app prints to (`06 Composites App/app/labels.js`; app README, Labels). Not bought as of 2026-10-10 |
| **Cost** | Not quoted yet: get a quote for the printer and rolls before the `/purchase` request. Size the roll order on ~480 labels per season (team estimate carried from Rev C; where it was measured is not recorded) |
| **Requested by** | Composites |

**Justification.** The shop's current identification method is handwriting on tape, and a standard Sharpie is soluble in the isopropyl alcohol used at every stage of CS-004 and CS-009. So the labels the team already relies on are being erased by the team's own cleaning step. A single mis-identified 8-ply carbon part costs roughly $300–600 in fabric and resin plus about 20 person-hours to remake (team estimate), and a mis-identified mold costs a machining slot at RFS. Payback is one prevented mix-up.

**Why not cheaper.** The zero-cost path (Avery sheets on the office laser with a packing-tape overlaminate, CS-001 §7.8) is retained as the documented fallback, not eliminated. It works; it is just slower per label and one grade less durable.

sections.title: CS-012 Purchasing & Reimbursement
sections.section: 7.9 Logging the purchase in the app
sections.text:
Every purchase should be logged in the Budget tab. Inventory's Incoming list, the Running out card's "on order" and a received lot's link back to its purchase all read from it, and none of them work for a purchase nobody logged (R6).

1. Press + New Purchase in Budget when you make the `/purchase` request. The app gives it a `BUY-SN6-###` ID.
2. Fill Item, Purchaser, Purpose, Cost ($) and Source / vendor, and write the bot's REQ number in Notes.
3. If the money is not composites', write the reference ID in Charged to, for example `TRAN-002` for RFS consumables, so the composites season total stays ours. Leave it blank for a `COMP-` line.
4. Add Line items with + Line, one per thing that will go on a shelf, with the total and count as the receipt prints them.

sections.title: CS-013 Work Orders & Part Traceability
sections.text: The Master Tracker did its job at the fleet level: parts, owners, deadlines, all visible. What it never gave us was the *part-level* record: steps, buy-offs, the stack as actually laid, measurements, photos. All of that lived in Slack threads and people's heads (PP-09). A work order (WO) is one run's complete record (a part has one run per attempt at making it, §4.1 rule 3), spec through blockers through execution through evidence, on a screen or printed and kept with the part.

sections.title: CS-013 Work Orders & Part Traceability
sections.text:
Every manufactured composites part and mold, including small cross-team jobs (the catch-can class of work, PP-05). If it consumes carbon or machine time, it gets a WO, with one carve-out: coupon-scale test pieces live on the app's R&D bench as studies and coupons (`RDS` / `CPN`, §4.1) with no work order, no traveler and no cure hold. The panel a coupon is cut from is still a build under this standard; the pieces cut from it are bench records.

Which record to make: test pieces you will cut, measure and compare (coupons, offcuts, trial panels you will not keep) should go in a study. Anything with a mold, a checklist or a cure you need to sign should be a part and a run, marked R&D if it is not for the car (§4). A study may also hold the parts and runs an effort produced, as a folder. Filing a part under a study does not make it R&D, and deleting a study ungroups its parts without deleting them.
