1. Clean the machined mold: dust off, then wipe with IPA on microfiber (CS-004 §7.1).
2. Inspect: every scribe line and datum crisp; photograph the dry mold; fill gouges per CS-003 (CS-004 §7.2).
3. Seal with XCR, 150 g or less per batch at 100:41 by weight (CS-004 §7.3).
4. Overcoat while the first coat is firm but tacky, checked with a fingernail (CS-004 §7.3 step 6).
5. Wait 12 h after the last coat, the FEB hold (CS-004 §7.3 step 7).
6. Wax with Formula Five: 4 coats minimum on a new mold, buffing between coats (CS-004 §7.4 step 1).
7. Wait at least 1 h after the last wax coat (CS-004 §7.4 step 2).
8. PVA with Partall #10: 2 coats, each dry before the next (CS-004 §7.4 step 3).
9. Record the seal on the mold and in the "Seal and release mold" note (CS-004 §7.4 step 5).
10. Label the back face and set Stage to Ready for layup (CS-004 §7.5).

QR-004 §2 to §8 cover each step in turn.

sections.title: QR-004 Mold sealing and release, in order
sections.section: 2. Cleaning a mold before sealing: IPA, never acetone
sections.text:
Clean a machined mold with 91% isopropyl alcohol on a microfiber cloth. Never acetone on tooling board, which attacks the board, and never fibrous shop towels, which leave strings in the surface (CS-004 §7.1).

Also called: cleaning, wipe down, IPA, isopropyl, rubbing alcohol, acetone, solvent, dust, mold cleaner.

1. Blow all dust off the mold with compressed air, including pockets and scribe lines (CS-004 §7.1 step 1).
2. Wipe the whole surface with an IPA-dampened microfiber cloth (CS-004 §7.1 step 2).
3. Repeat with a clean face of the cloth until it comes away clean.
4. From here on, handle the mold with gloves only. Skin oils contaminate the surface (CS-004 §7.1 step 3).

Which IPA: the 91% isopropyl bottle, which the app records as "Isopropyl alcohol 91%". Never the 70% rubbing alcohol (CS-004 §5).

Acetone and fibrous towels are both failure modes the team documented in SN4 (CS-004 §7.1).

A re-used mold that is already sealed is cleaned with Formula Five Clean 'N Glaze, then gets 1–2 wax coats and PVA (CS-004 §7.4 step 4; QR-004 §7).

sections.title: QR-004 Mold sealing and release, in order
sections.section: 3. Mixing XCR to seal a mold: batch size and ratio
sections.text:
Mix XCR 150 g or less at a time, at 100:41 resin to hardener by weight. Pot life at that size is 8 minutes at 20 °C and 4 at 30 °C, and a bigger batch is shorter-lived and hotter (CS-004 §7.3 step 2).

Also called: XCR, sealer, mold sealer, seal coat, coating resin, batch size, mixing XCR.

1. Check the room is 15–30 °C and can stay at 20 °C or warmer through the cure (CS-004 §7.3 step 1).
2. Check both jugs are inside 15–30 °C. On a cold night, bring them in from storage first.
3. Avoid a humid room. Do not seal outdoors on cold evenings: the datasheet rates XCR for 15–30 °C only (CS-004 §7.3 step 1).
4. Weigh XCR at 100:41 resin to hardener by weight, 150 g or less (CS-004 §7.3 steps 2 and 3).
5. Mix at least 2 min, scraping walls and base.
6. Double-pot: transfer to a second cup and remix with a fresh stick.
7. Write each batch mass on the work order.

A 150 g batch covers roughly a medium mold section per coat. Mix again rather than mixing big (CS-004 §7.3 step 2).

Anyone who has had a skin reaction to epoxy shall not mix or brush XCR, and tells a lead (CS-004 §6). Nitrile gloves and safety glasses with side shields whenever XCR is open (CS-004 §6). Unmixed streaks from the cup walls are the classic soft-spot cause (CS-004 §7.3 step 3).

sections.title: QR-004 Mold sealing and release, in order
sections.section: 4. How many XCR coats, and when to put on the second coat (fingernail test)
sections.text:
Usually two coats on 30 lb board, often one on 60 lb, two on 45 lb (team rule); a mixed-grade mold seals like its softest board (CS-004 §7.3 step 4). Overcoat when the first coat is firm but tacky (fingernail dents it), about 2 h 50 at 20 °C (CS-004 §7.3 step 6).

Also called: second coat, recoat, overcoat, fingernail test, firm but tacky, B-stage, tack-free, how many coats.

How many coats: 30 lb board usually needs a second coat, and 60 lb board often seals in one. Plan two coats on 45 lb board until the team has a record of it sealing in one (team rule). A mold cut from mixed grades seals like its softest board, so you should plan two coats if any of it is 30 or 45 lb. The mold's "Board density, min" and "Board density, max" fields show the range (CS-004 §7.3 step 4).

1. Brush a thin, even coat over the working surface and flanges (CS-004 §7.3 step 4).
2. Work resin out of corners and fillets. A pool in a crevice is the Duratec failure.
3. Watch the scribe lines. If one floods, drag the brush along it before the resin gels (CS-004 §7.3 step 5).
4. Press a fingernail into the first coat on the flange. Firm but tacky means overcoat now; it bonds with no prep (CS-004 §7.3 step 6).

At 30 °C the window comes at about 1 h 30. Either time is an estimate, and the fingernail decides (CS-004 §7.3 step 6). Missed the window and the coat is tack-free: QR-004 §5.

sections.title: QR-004 Mold sealing and release, in order
sections.section: 5. First coat went tack-free? Sanding XCR before the next coat
sections.text:
If the first coat has gone tack-free (coming back another day always means tack-free), wait at least 9 h from application, then key it with 120 grit before recoating (CS-004 §7.3 step 6). Firm-but-tacky XCR needs no sanding.

Also called: sand XCR, sanding XCR, key, scuff, 120 grit, missed the overcoat window, recoat next day, tack-free, second coat next day.

1. Wait at least 9 h from application (CS-004 §7.3 step 6).
2. Key the surface with 120 grit.
3. Blow off the dust.
4. Wipe with IPA.
5. Recoat, mixing 150 g or less at 100:41 by weight (CS-004 §7.3 steps 2 and 3).

sections.title: QR-004 Mold sealing and release, in order
sections.section: 6. How long after XCR before wax? The 12 h hold
sections.text:
Wait 12 h after the last XCR coat before the wax and PVA go on. That is the team's FEB hold; the datasheet initial cure is 8 h 30 at 20 °C, handleable at about 9 h (CS-004 §7.3 step 7). The app does not lock this hold, so watch it yourself.

Also called: XCR cure time, seal cure, how long to cure the sealer, 12 hours, FEB hold, when can I wax.

1. Write the last-coat time in the note on the work order's "Seal and release mold" step (CS-004 §7.3 step 7).
2. Wait 12 h from that time.
3. Press a fingernail into the flange, not the part surface. Pass is no mark (CS-004 §8).
4. Only if a run or nib formed: denib it locally with 800 grit or finer (a team value), then wipe with IPA (CS-004 §7.3 step 7).
5. Keep water off the sealed surface for 24 h after application (CS-004 §7.3 step 8).

Check the scribe lines against the photo of the dry mold: all of them identifiable, and no glossy pools in fillets or corners under raking light (CS-004 §8).

sections.title: QR-004 Mold sealing and release, in order
sections.section: 7. Wax then PVA: coats, and how long each must dry
sections.text:
New mold: Formula Five wax, 4 coats minimum, buffing between coats, a wait of at least 1 h, then Partall #10 PVA, 2 coats, each dry before the next, about 15–45 min a coat (CS-004 §7.4; `03 Datasheets/PARTALL-Film-10.pdf`).

Also called: release, release agent, mold release, wax, Formula Five, PVA, Partall, Clean 'N Glaze, mold cleaner, re-wax.

1. Check the 12 h hold after the last XCR coat has passed (CS-004 §7.4 step 1).
2. Wipe on a thin film of Formula Five wax.
3. Let it haze.
4. Buff with a clean microfiber.
5. Repeat for 4 coats minimum on a new mold. The 4 is the team's count; the Formula Five guide asks for at least three on a new mold (`03 Datasheets/FORMULA-FIVE-Mold-Release-Wax.pdf`).
6. Wait at least 1 h after the last wax coat, so its solvents out-gas before the PVA (CS-004 §7.4 step 2).
7. Apply Partall #10 PVA in thin, even coats (CS-004 §7.4 step 3).
8. Let each coat dry fully to a glossy film. The Partall guide gives about 15–45 minutes a coat, depending on temperature, humidity and thickness (CS-004 §7.4 step 3).
9. Two coats. The 2 is the team's count; the Partall guide gives a mist coat then flow coats on a new mold.

Re-used sealed mold: clean with Clean 'N Glaze, then 1–2 wax coats, the 1 h wait and PVA as above (CS-004 §7.4 step 4).

Check: continuous PVA gloss with no fisheyes or dry patches (CS-004 §8). A dull, hazy or grainy PVA film can mean the coat is too thin (Partall guide).

sections.title: QR-004 Mold sealing and release, in order
sections.section: 8. When is the mold Ready for layup? Recording and labeling it
sections.text:
A mold is ready when it is sealed, released, recorded and labeled, and its Stage is set to Ready for layup. Then it is cleared for infusion (CS-006) or wet layup (CS-007) (CS-004 §7.5 step 5).

Also called: ready for layup, mold label, mould label, sticker, Sealed on, Stage, mold record, identify.

1. On the Molds tab, open the mold (CS-004 §7.4 step 5).
2. Set Sealing system to XCR, Sealed on to the date of the last XCR coat, Sealed by to yourself, and Stage to Sealed.
3. In the "Seal and release mold" note, write the XCR batch masses, coat count and coat times, and the wax and PVA coat counts.
4. Pick a label patch on the back face, inboard of the 40 mm keep-out at every edge, so never within 40 mm of the flange perimeter (CS-004 §7.5 step 1).
5. Scuff the patch to 220 grit and wipe with IPA (CS-004 §7.5 step 2).
6. Print the mold's label from the app and apply it. Check its parts-pulled count, seal date and sealed-by name (CS-004 §7.5 step 3).
7. Check the engraved mold ID is still legible; re-engrave or stamp it if not (CS-004 §7.5 step 4).
8. Set Stage to Ready for layup (CS-004 §7.5 step 5).

Labeling is last on purpose: a label put on before the XCR gets brushed over or peeled off, and a label edge under the seal is a leak channel you will not find at 27 inHg (CS-004 §7.5). On a re-seal, print a new label with the new seal date and the incremented parts-pulled count.

sections.title: QR-005 Which label goes where
sections.text:
Mold: back face, engraved ID plus a 5522 label. Part: trim area at demould, then a hidden face. Chemical container with a UC EH&S tag: no FEB label. Shelf: front edge. Mixed pot: tape and marker (CS-001 §7.2).

Also called: label, sticker, tag; QR, QR code, barcode; where does the label go, labelling, labeling.

| Object | Where it goes | Media (CS-001 §7.2) |
|---|---|---|
| Mold | Back face, inboard of the 40 mm keep-out at every edge. Never the working surface or the flange | Engraved ID plus a printed 5522 label |
| Part, at demould | Trim area, bag side, inside the CAD trim line | Printed, permanent adhesive |
| Part, after trim | A hidden face, 25 mm or more from any DP420 bond line | 5522, before clear coat |
| Test panel | Bag side, in the offcut margin; coupon IDs marked across the cut lines | Printed plus paint marker |
| Tensile coupon | Paint marker on the tab only; the `CPN` label goes on its bag or tag | Marker plus printed label |
| R&D study | The bag, tray or box its coupons live in | Printed |
| Fabric roll | A tag through the core, on wire or a zip tie | Printed label on the tag |
| Fabric offcut bag | On the bag, with the remaining length in paint marker beside it | Printed plus marker |
| Chemical container with an EH&S tag | No FEB label; record the tag in EH&S barcode | Campus tag |
| Chemical container with no tag yet | On the container | 5522 only |
| Consumable (cups, bag film, tape) | The box or bin, one label per record | Printed |
| Tooling board sheet | Paint marker on the face, 15 mm characters | Marker |
| Tooling board blank, cut and not yet glued | Paint marker: mold ID (or plan name) and layer tag, before it leaves the saw | Marker |
| Board remnant | ID in paint marker plus the printed board label on a taped tag | Marker plus tag |
| Storage location | Front edge of the shelf, readable standing up | Printed |
| Jig, fixture | A non-clamping face | Printed |

Issues, purchases, documents and stack plans never get a label (CS-001 §2).

sections.title: QR-005 Which label goes where
sections.section: 2. Where does the label go on a mold?
sections.text:
On the back face, inboard of the 40 mm keep-out at every edge, and never on the working surface or within 40 mm of the flange perimeter on either face (CS-001 §6 rules 1 and 2; §7.2). The printed label goes on only after sealing is finished (CS-001 §7.4).

Also called: mold label, mould label, tool ID, engraving, engraved ID, keep-out zone.

Before glue-up, each blank is marked as it comes off the saw with its mold ID (or the plan name) and its layer tag from the cut sheet (L1, L2b), in paint marker (CS-001 §7.4).

A mold is identified three times (CS-001 §7.4):

1. At glue-up, write the mold ID (`MOLD-SN6-###`), the part name, the WO and an up arrow in paint marker, 15 mm characters, on two adjacent side faces of the glued stack.
2. At machining, engrave the mold ID on the back face: 6 mm cap height, 1.0 mm deep, single-line font, 3.175 mm ball or 90° V-bit. The engraving is the record of record.
3. At the end of sealing, after the fourth wax coat is buffed and the PVA is dry, scuff a patch of the back face to 220 grit.
4. Wipe the patch with IPA.
5. Apply the printed 5522 label to the patch.

Why the keep-outs: anything on the tool face telegraphs into the part, and tacky tape is 12.7 mm wide, so a label edge under the seal is a leak channel (CS-001 §6).

> Do not apply the printed label before sealing. It gets brushed over with XCR, or peeled off leaving adhesive XCR will not wet out (CS-001 §7.4).

When a mold is stripped and re-sealed, print a new label with the new seal date and parts-pulled count (CS-001 §7.4).

sections.title: QR-005 Which label goes where
sections.section: 3. Labeling a part at demould (demold): why two labels?
sections.text:
At demould, print two identical labels on 5522. Label A goes on the trim area, bag side, inside the CAD trim line. Label B is stapled to the work order traveler and goes on a hidden face after sanding (CS-001 §7.5).

Also called: demould, demold, de-mould; labeling, labelling; part label, part sticker; traveler, traveller.

Do not peel and re-stick a label. A label peeled off a demoulded part carries wax and PVA on its adhesive (CS-001 §7.5).

1. At demould, print two identical labels on 5522.
2. Apply label A to the trim area on the bag side, inside the CAD trim line.
3. Staple label B to the work order traveler.
4. At trim, label A is cut off with the trim and binned. The traveler now carries the part's identity.
5. After sanding and before clear coat, apply label B to the scuffed, IPA-wiped hidden face, 25 mm or more from any DP420 bond line (CS-001 §7.2).
6. Clear coat goes over label B where the geometry allows.

On a sheet the app prints one label per record, so the second label is a second print. On a roll, Copies of each set to 2 prints the pair, but roll stock is thermal paper, so a roll pair only suits a part that will not be wiped or clear-coated (CS-001 §7.5).

sections.title: QR-005 Which label goes where
sections.section: 4. Which label stock: paper, 5522 polyester or the roll?
sections.text:
Anything that will see IPA, acetone or resin shall get a 5522 polyester label (or an overlaminated sheet label), never thermal roll stock (DK-2210, DK-1201). Roll stock is for shelves, bins, dry fabric and consumables only (CS-001 §7.2 stock rule).

Also called: label stock, Avery 5161, Avery 5522, polyester label, weatherproof label, thermal roll, Brother label, DK-2210.

| Stock | Use it for | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Avery 5161 paper sheet | Everyday dry things | CS-001 §5 |
| Avery 5522 polyester sheet | Untagged chemical containers, parts, molds, anything that sees IPA, acetone or resin | CS-001 §5, §7.2 |
| DK-2210 or DK-1201 thermal roll | Shelves, bins, dry fabric, consumables | CS-001 §5, §7.2 |

Thermal paper fades in UV, blackens with heat and smears under solvent (CS-001 §7.2). The Label button prints on the media this device is set to, under Reports → Label media. To print one record on a different stock, open the Print labels builder and pick it under Media (CS-001 §7.1).

sections.title: QR-005 Which label goes where
sections.section: 5. What does a material lot label say?
sections.text:
The name and the ID, then one bold key line. For resin and hardener with no EH&S tag: the vendor lot number and opened date sit under the bold mix ratio and role; received date, expiry and shelf go in the footer (CS-001 §7.6).

Also called: lot label, material label, jug label, roll label, resin label, what's on the label.

| Class | What the label carries (CS-001 §7.6) |
|---|---|
| Part, test panel | The layup stack in CS-002 shorthand |
| Mold | The sealing record: sealed date, by whom, parts pulled, revision |
| Fabric | Vendor lot number on the detail line; received date and shelf in the footer. Dry fabric has no expiry field |
| Resin, hardener, consumable with no EH&S tag | Vendor lot and opened date under the mix ratio and role; received date, expiry and shelf in the footer |
| Board, remnant | Density in the key line; dimensions and quantity; the mold it came off and its shelf |
| Storage location | STORAGE; site and kind, and FLAMMABLES OK when the shelf is rated |

A container wearing an EH&S tag gets no FEB label at all (CS-001 §7.2).

The vendor lot and expiry print from whatever the record holds. If ✨ Read label filled them, check them against the container before you print (CS-001 §7.6).

An R&D build carries `R&D` in a box on the ID line. It means not a season deliverable, not scrap (CS-001 §7.6).

sections.title: QR-005 Which label goes where
sections.section: 6. Chemical containers and the UC EH&S tag
sections.text:
A chemical container wearing a UC EH&S tag gets no FEB label. The campus tag is its label: record the tag in the lot's EH&S barcode field so scanning it opens the FEB record (CS-001 §7.11).

Also called: EH&S tag, UC tag, RSS tag, campus barcode, Data Matrix, chemical tag.

1. At receiving, scan or type each container's tag into the EH&S tag cell of its line on the Receiving desk (CS-001 §7.11 step 1; QR-006).
2. For a container already on a shelf, open its record, press Edit, and press the scan button beside EH&S barcode, or type the code.
3. If the face of the tag is scuffed, type the twelve characters printed down its right edge. If two containers share those twelve, the app asks for more of the code (CS-001 §7.11 step 3).
4. One tag, one container. The app refuses a tag another record already wears; fix the wrong record.
5. A code that is not 24 characters saves with a warning. Check it against the tag.
6. A chemical container with no tag yet gets a 5522 FEB label. When campus tags it, record the tag and leave the FEB label on (CS-001 §7.11 step 7).

Fabric lots have no EH&S barcode field: dry fabric is not in the campus chemical system (CS-001 §7.11).

sections.title: QR-005 Which label goes where
sections.section: 7. No label printer, or the printer is broken
sections.text:
Print the label sheet on plain paper from the app, cut it on the guillotine, and overlaminate with 3 in clear packing tape overlapping the label by at least 6 mm on all four sides (CS-001 §7.8). This is the documented path, not a degraded one.

Also called: no printer, printer broken, printer not showing, overlaminate, packing tape label, paint marker.

1. Print the label sheet on plain paper from the app.
2. Cut on the guillotine, on the crop marks. Not with scissors.
3. Overlaminate with 3 in clear packing tape, overlapping the label by at least 6 mm on all four sides.
4. Burnish hard with a thumbnail.

Tape flush to the label edge lets solvent wick under, and it delaminates in a week (CS-001 §7.8). For anything tag-able, a laminating pouch on a zip tie seals all four edges; punch through the sealed margin, never the paper.

When the printer breaks, in order (CS-001 §7.9):

1. Use the spare roll taped to the printer. Most "broken printer" reports are an empty or jammed roll, or a printer off the shed wifi.
2. Print Avery 5161 on the office laser through the app, with the overlaminate above.
3. Paint marker on masking tape. Never scannable, acceptable for 72 hours.

sections.title: QR-005 Which label goes where
sections.section: 8. Labeling a mixed pot or an opened container
sections.text:
Never print a label for a mixed pot. Write on the cup with tape and marker: product, time mixed (HHMM, 24 h) and initials, plus batch mass where CS-004 §7.3 requires it (CS-001 §7.7).

Also called: labeling, labelling; pot label, mixing cup, mixed resin, cup label, opened sticker, write-on tape.

A pot of XCR has an 8 minute pot life at 20 °C (CS-001 §7.7, from CS-004 §7.3). Standing at a printer burns that time. Write it like this (CS-001 §7.7):

```
IN2 2142 JS product · time mixed (HHMM, 24 h) · initials
XCR 0906 SS 140g add batch mass where CS-004 §7.3 requires it
```

Anything unlabelled and curing is treated as hot waste (CS-001 §7.7, CS-008).

Anything opened that has no lot record gets an opened sticker: `OPEN 2026-10-14 JS` (CS-001 §7.7). A container that has a lot record does not need one: press Open on its page and the app stamps the Opened date (CS-014 §7.8).

Use an oil-based paint marker for every hand mark, never a Sharpie. A standard Sharpie dissolves in IPA, and the process wipes with IPA at every stage (CS-001 §5).

sections.title: QR-006 Receiving a delivery and material lots
sections.section: 1. How do I log a delivery?
sections.text:
On Inventory, press Receive a delivery to open the Receiving desk. Set Supplier and Arrived, add one row per kind of thing, press Review N records, then Create N records. Log it the day it arrives (CS-014 §8).

Also called: receive, receiving, delivery, package, box, order arrived, log a delivery, check in stock.

1. Open the desk: Inventory → Storage map → Receive a delivery. From a line on the Incoming card, Arrived ▸ fills the whole order in for you (CS-014 §7.2).
2. If the desk shows "In the last hour: [name] added N. Same delivery?", ask that person before you type anything.
3. Set Supplier.
4. Set Arrived to the day the delivery came in. It becomes every record's Received date.
5. Set New lines land on to the shelf most of the delivery goes to.
6. Start a row and pick its Class first: Fabric, Resin, Hardener or Consumable.
7. Put a kit's resin and hardener on separate rows, Resin and Hardener.
8. Type What is it as the container names it, and How many.
9. Set Shelf on any row going somewhere other than the default.
10. Type Vendor lot exactly as printed, or leave it blank if nothing is printed.
11. Fill EH&S tag and Expires (QR-006 §3 and §5).
12. Type $ each, the price of one unit.
13. Press Enter to start the next row.
14. Press Review N records, check the list and its warnings, then press Create N records (QR-006 §6).
15. If the rows came from Arrived ▸ or Take all, they carry no Material type: press Link materials on the Materials list afterwards (CS-014 §7.3 step 6).

If you leave before finishing, the sheet is kept on this device for 24 hours and Inventory shows "Finish N lines" (CS-014 §7.2 step 4). It is not shared with anyone else's device.

Tooling board does not go through the desk. Log it under Inventory → Boards (CS-014 §2).

sections.title: QR-006 Receiving a delivery and material lots
sections.section: 2. One record per roll or jug: how many records will a row make?
sections.text:
Fabric, Resin and Hardener rows make one record per roll or container: How many 3 makes 3 records. A Consumable row makes one record carrying the count, "1 of 50" (CS-014 §4; §7.3 step 7).

Also called: lot, batch, jug, roll, container, one record each, how many records, count.

A lot is one record for one physical thing on a shelf (CS-014 §4). The IDs are `FAB-SN6-###` for fabric, `RSN-SN6-###` for resin and hardener (the record's Role says which), and `CON-SN6-###` for consumables, each with its own counter.

The desk refuses more than 50 tracked units on one row (CS-014 §7.3 step 7). Split the row, or log a box of small items as one Consumable with a count.

Why one per jug: the cure buy-off asks which resin lot and which hardener lot went into the part, and pre-fills the most recently opened lot of each class (CS-014 §7.8). Two jugs on one record make that answer meaningless.

A row with no shelf lands in No location on the storage map. Put it away the same day (CS-014 §7.3 step 8).

If you paste a block copied from an order email, each line becomes a row. Check the Class, How many and Shelf of every pasted row (CS-014 §7.3 step 13).

sections.title: QR-006 Receiving a delivery and material lots
sections.section: 3. Where do the lot number and expiry date come from?
sections.text:
Vendor lot: type it exactly as printed on the container or slip, blank if none. Expires: type it off the container. Fabric has no expiry field. The lot's Expiry from field says where a date came from (CS-014 §4; §7.3 step 9; §7.7).

Also called: lot number, batch number, vendor lot; expiry, expiration, expiry date, use-by, best before, shelf life.

Expiry from has three values (CS-014 §4):

| Expiry from | Meaning |
|---|---|
| vendor label | A person typed it |
| vendor label (AI read) | A ✨ read set it and nobody has typed over it |
| shelf-life table | Link materials worked it out from Received plus the TDS shelf life |

1. At the desk, type Expires off the container for every resin, hardener and chemical consumable that prints one (CS-014 §7.7 step 1).
2. If the container prints only a manufacture date and a shelf life, work out the expiry (manufacture date plus shelf life) and type it into Expires (step 2).
3. Link materials on the Materials list fills a blank Expires from Received plus the TDS shelf life, but only on records with no Material type (imports, old records, rows filled by Arrived ▸). It never changes a filled field, and it does not reach a lot the desk already typed (step 3).
4. Where the label gives a date, type it over a shelf-life date. A shelf-life date counts from the day we received the container, so it can run later than the maker's date (step 4).

The shelf lives in the table are datasheet figures: IN2 and AT30 12 months (`03 Datasheets/EC-TDS-IN2-Infusion-Resin.pdf`), XCR 12 months (`03 Datasheets/EC-TDS-XCR-Epoxy-Coating-Resin.pdf`), when stored as the TDS says, and DP420 24 months from manufacture (`03 Datasheets/3m-scotch-weld-epoxy-adhesive-dp420-black.pdf`, p.5) (CS-014 §7.7 step 3).

To read a container's label with the camera, open the lot's page and press ✨ Read label. In the "From the label" sheet, untick anything that does not match the container, then press Apply (CS-014 §7.7 steps 5 and 6).

sections.title: QR-006 Receiving a delivery and material lots
sections.section: 4. What does ✨ From packing slip do, and why check every row?
sections.text:
It reads a photo or PDF of the slip and adds one row per shipped line: name, quantity shipped, and vendor lot and expiry only where the slip prints them. Anything a ✨ button fills is a draft: the person saving it shall check every row against the paper (CS-014 §7.4).

Also called: packing slip, delivery note, AI read, AI fill, sparkle button, scan the slip, read the slip.

The button shows under the sheet only when a lead has AI features on. Class, Material type, supplier and cost come from the app's own tables, never from the model. An expiry printed as month and year is read as the last day of that month (CS-014 §7.4).

1. Press ✨ From packing slip and photograph the slip, or pick its PDF.
2. Wait for "N lines read from the slip. Check the class, the shelf and the count on each."
3. Check every row against the slip and against what is physically in the box: Class, What is it, How many, Vendor lot, Expires.
4. Fix a wrong cell by typing in it.
5. Remove any row for something not in the box with the bin icon (Remove this line).
6. Where the container prints an expiry, type it into Expires from the container. That clears the AI mark.
7. If the read fails or finds no lines, type the rows or paste them from the order email.

An AI-read expiry stays marked "vendor label (AI read)" until a person types over it, and an AI read is never a source for a number in a standard (CS-014 §7.4). The photo is deleted as soon as it is read (CS-014 §5).

Each person gets 50 photo reads a day, shared by receipts, packing slips and container labels (CS-014 §5).

sections.title: QR-006 Receiving a delivery and material lots
sections.section: 5. Recording the EH&S tag when a delivery arrives
sections.text:
For each Resin, Hardener or chemical Consumable row, press the camera button in the EH&S tag cell and scan the tag on every container in the row. One code per container: the number of codes on a row equals How many (CS-014 §7.6).

Also called: EH&S tag, UC tag, RSS tag, campus barcode, chemical barcode, Data Matrix.

1. Press the camera button in the row's EH&S tag cell. The camera stays open; each scan adds a code.
2. Scan the tag on each container in the row.
3. If the camera fails, type all 24 characters from the face of the tag. Separate several codes with spaces.
4. Do not record a new container by its 12-character edge print. Typed at receipt, it saves a short code that will not match the RSS inventory (CS-014 §7.6 step 3).
5. Count the codes against How many. One code on a multi-container row raises no warning, so count them yourself (step 4).
6. Count each code's characters against the tag. The desk does not check length, and a short code saves anyway (step 6).
7. If the confirm says a tag is already on another record, that container is already tracked. Take it off the sheet (step 5).

A chemical container with no tag yet: leave the cell blank and give it a 5522 FEB label. When campus tags it, record the tag on its record and leave the FEB label on (CS-014 §7.6 step 7).

Cups, gloves, bag film and other non-chemical consumables have no tag. Leave the cell blank (step 8).

Tagged containers get no FEB label: the tag is the label (CS-001 §7.2; QR-005).

sections.title: QR-006 Receiving a delivery and material lots
sections.text:
Press Review N records (or Ctrl+Enter), untick anything that did not turn up, read every warning, then press Create N records. The bar "N records added" offers Print N labels and Undo. Labels are never printed automatically (CS-014 §7.5).

Also called: confirm, create records, print labels, undo receiving, review.

1. Press Review N records. The confirm "Create N records?" lists the rows by shelf.
2. Untick anything that did not actually turn up.
3. Read every warning: EH&S tag counts that do not fit, a tag already on another record, flammable items landing on a shelf not rated for them. Fix them with Back to the sheet.
4. Press Create N records. Every record starts Sealed, dated with Arrived.
5. If the batch has no EH&S-tagged containers, press Print N labels.
6. If it has tagged containers, print from Inventory → Labels instead, with What set to Material lots.
7. Tick only the records without a tag and press Preview N labels.
8. If something is wrong, press Undo. It deletes the records just made and puts the rows back on the sheet. Bin any labels already printed for them.

With no connection the app cannot get IDs, writes nothing and says so. Try again when back online (CS-014 §7.5 step 4).

When every line of a purchase is in, set its Order status to Arrived on the Budget tab. Receiving does not change it (CS-014 §7.5 step 11).

sections.title: QR-006 Receiving a delivery and material lots
sections.text:
The receiver shall set Hazard on every resin, hardener and chemical consumable lot the day it is received: open the lot's page, press Edit, set Hazard. Receiving does not set it yet (CS-014 §6 step 4).

Also called: hazard, flammable, flammables, not flammable, flash point, SDS, fire risk.

Read it off the SDS §2. Pick "flammable" when the SDS lists a flammable gas, aerosol or liquid (GHS H220 to H226, or an older OSHA Class I flammable liquid), otherwise "not flammable" (CS-014 §6 step 4). Blank means unknown, and an unknown lot cannot trigger the storage map's flammables warning (CS-014 §4).

| Material | Hazard (CS-014 §6, from the SDS) |
|---|---|
| IN2 resin, AT30 SLOW, AT30 FAST | not flammable |
| XCR resin and hardener | not flammable |
| West 105 resin; 205, 206, 209 hardeners | not flammable |
| Airtac 2 spray | flammable |
| LiME LiNE UC4:1 Part A | flammable |
| Acetone | flammable |
| 91% IPA | flammable |

Hazard records what the SDS says. Which cabinet a material lives in is CS-011 §6's call (CS-014 §6). Co-storage: see CS-011 §6; under review.

The desk's confirm warns that flammable items would land on a location that is not rated only for a Material type whose restock rule a lead has marked flammable. None of the shipped rules is, so today the desk does not warn. It does not read the lot's Hazard; set Hazard from the SDS as above (CS-014 §6).

sections.title: QR-006 Receiving a delivery and material lots
sections.section: 8. Damaged or leaking container at delivery
sections.text:
Wear nitrile gloves when you unpack and shelve chemical containers. Do not receive a leaking container onto a shelf: leave it in its packaging, set it apart from other chemicals, read its SDS and tell a lead (CS-014 §6 steps 1 and 2).

Also called: leaking, damaged, broken jug, spill, cracked container, leaking delivery.

Chemicals go straight onto a location CS-011 §6 allows for them, never a fridge (CS-014 §6 step 3). Nitrile gloves are shop stock (CS-014 §5).

sections.title: QR-006 Receiving a delivery and material lots
sections.section: 9. Part of the order came, or donated or sponsor stock
sections.text:
Receive only what came; the rest stays on Incoming as N of M in. Donated, sponsor or legacy stock goes through Receive a delivery with the donor in Supplier and $ each blank (CS-014 §7.5 step 10; §7.11).

Also called: donated, donor, donation, sponsor stock, legacy stock, partial delivery, part of the order, short shipped, backorder.

Part of the order came:

1. Receive only what came (CS-014 §7.5 step 10).
2. The rest stays on Incoming as "N of M in · K to come".
3. If a line will never arrive, tell a lead. The app has no button to close a line short yet (CS-014 §7.1 step 4).

Donated, sponsor or legacy stock (CS-014 §7.11):

1. Receive it through the desk from Receive a delivery, like any delivery. There is no purchase, so no Arrived ▸.
2. Name the sponsor or donor in Supplier.
3. Leave $ each blank. Donated stock stays un-costed.
4. For legacy stock found on a shelf with no record, set Arrived to the day you log it.
5. Set Hazard, the EH&S tag and Expires on chemical containers as in QR-006 §3, §5 and §7.

sections.title: QR-007 Work orders: steps, buy-offs, holds and issues
sections.section: 1. Part or run: what is the difference, and which do I make?
sections.text:
A part (`P-SN6-###`) is the thing the car needs. A run (`WO-SN6-###`) is one attempt at making it; the Work Orders tab calls a run a work order. Make the part first, then press + New run on it (CS-013 §4; §7.1).

Also called: WO, work order, run, traveler, traveller, job; part, P number; remake, re-lay, second attempt.

A part has many runs, and each run belongs to one part (CS-013 §4). A re-laid part is a new run on the same part, never a new part: dispose the issue on the failed run as Scrap, then press + New run (CS-013 §4.1 rule 3). The part keeps its `P` ID and every label stays valid.

| You are making | You should make (CS-013 §2) |
|---|---|
| A part for the car | A part on the Parts tab, then a run |
| Something with a mold, a checklist or a cure to sign, not for the car | A part and a run started from the R&D tab (an R&D part) |
| Coupons, offcuts or trial panels you will cut, measure and compare | A study on the R&D tab, with no work order |
| A one-off job that will never be remade | New WO on the Work Orders tab (a run with no part) |

An R&D part keeps every blocker, hold and evidence check: they work exactly as on a season part. It is kept off the Season tab and the Parts and Work Orders lists and lives on the R&D tab (CS-013 §4).

sections.title: QR-007 Work orders: steps, buy-offs, holds and issues
sections.text:
On the Parts tab press New Part (or open the part), fill its requirements, then press + New run. The run gets `WO-SN6-###` and copies the part's plan: engineers, deadline, mass target, technique, stack and BOM (CS-013 §7.1).

Also called: new work order, new WO, new run, create a work order, start a job.

1. Make the part on the Parts tab with New Part, or open the part if it exists.
2. Fill the part's requirements before any work: Subteam, Layup type, Layup deadline, Mold Engineer, Manufacturing Engineer, Target weight (g), the Layup stack (CS-002 §7.1) and Materials (plan).
3. Press + New run on the part.
4. For a remake, choose Use a previous run and pick what to keep. Start fresh copies the part's own plan.
5. On the run, set the quality checks with numeric targets in Quality (+ check). Mass is prefilled from Target weight.

The run's steps come from its technique, which the Layup type picks (CS-013 §7.1 step 5). If the checklist does not fit the job, fix the technique, not the run: pick the right Layup type before the run starts, or ask a lead to add a technique. Members cannot delete steps. A step that does not apply is signed with a note saying why.

Person fields (Mold Engineer, Manufacturing Engineer, Laid up by) are picked from the app's roster, not typed (CS-013 §4).

sections.title: QR-007 Work orders: steps, buy-offs, holds and issues
sections.text:
Anyone signed in on the roster can buy off a step, including their own work, with two exceptions: a step that needs training needs someone a lead has recorded as trained, and Mold design review needs someone other than the mold's designer (CS-013 §4).

Also called: buy-off, buy off, sign-off, sign off, sign, initials, approve a step, who can sign.

The button on a step reads "buy off as [your name]". The app stores the signer's name, account, and the date and time. Treat it as "who was signed in when this was clicked", not a notarised signature (CS-013 §4).

1. Training to sign: the step can be bought off only by someone holding that training on the People tab. A lead may sign without it and must write why; the reason goes in the run's event log (CS-013 §4).
2. Independent design review: Mold design review shall be bought off by someone other than the part's Mold Engineer (CS-013 §4). The app only warns ("Self-review", with Sign it anyway) when the run's Mold Engineer signs; it never refuses, so the signer still checks who drew the CAD.
3. View as guest changes nothing, because every buy-off carries a name (CS-013 §5).

Each step gets a buy-off, a note and photos. Press the camera on the step row (Add photos to this step) to attach photos from your phone; a photo is never required (CS-013 §7.2 step 2).

Which training each step needs is in QR-007 §4.

sections.title: QR-007 Work orders: steps, buy-offs, holds and issues
sections.section: 4. Which training does each step need?
sections.text:
Mold design review needs Mold design. Glue and machining steps need ShopSabre CNC. Infusion steps need Resin infusion. Wet layup steps need Wet layup. Shape foam core needs Foam core (CS-013 §7.5 table).

Also called: training, trained, qualification, signed off to use, CNC training, ShopSabre training, infusion training.

| Technique | Step | Training (CS-013 §7.5) |
|---|---|---|
| Mold infusion, Mold wet lay | Mold design review | Mold design |
| Mold infusion | Glue mold stock; Machine mold | ShopSabre CNC |
| Mold wet lay | Glue and machine mold | ShopSabre CNC |
| Mold infusion, Glass infusion | Dry stack and bag; Drop test; Infuse | Resin infusion |
| Mold wet lay | Wet layup and bag | Wet layup |
| Foam wrapped | Shape foam core | Foam core |
| Foam wrapped | Wet layup over core | Wet layup |

A lead records who holds a training on the People tab. A lead is not trained by being a lead (CS-013 §4). The app's ShopSabre CNC training mirrors the RFS record, which CS-005 §4 names as the authority.

Every other built-in step (Stack frozen, Seal and release mold, Cure and demould, Trim and finish and the rest) needs no training. Their checks are blockers, evidence and the cure hold (QR-007 §5 and §6).

The table is the built-in techniques as the app shipped them on 2026-10-10. A lead can edit techniques; Reports → Layup techniques shows the live ones (CS-013 §7.5).

sections.title: QR-007 Work orders: steps, buy-offs, holds and issues
sections.section: 5. Why can't I sign this step? Blockers, evidence and OnHold
sections.text:
A blocker step blocks every step after it until someone buys it off. The blockers are Stack frozen, Mold design review, the drop test, and the acceptance criterion on an Other run. Some steps also need evidence before they can be signed (CS-013 §4).

Also called: blocked, blocker, locked step, greyed out, can't buy off, evidence, stack freeze, drop test, design review, OnHold, on hold, parked.

The run shows "Blocked by an unsigned blocker:" and names the step. Sign that one first.

| Step | What it needs before it can be signed (CS-013 §4, §7.5) |
|---|---|
| Stack frozen | A layup stack on the run |
| Mold design review | The CAD, attached or linked, plus Mold design training |
| Machine mold, Glue and machine mold | A note |
| Drop test, 1 inHg or less over 10 min | A note with the reading (the number is CS-006 §7.4's) |
| Define acceptance criterion (Other) | A note: target and method, set before work starts |

A lead can sign without the evidence, with a written reason (CS-013 §4).

A technique that lays up a stack shall keep Stack frozen ahead of the first physical step, and a drop-test blocker ahead of the resin step (CS-013 §7.5 step 4). Mold wet lay and Foam wrapped have no drop-test step; on those the start and end readings go in the note on "Wet layup and bag" ("Wet layup over core" on a Foam wrapped run) (CS-007 §7.5).

OnHold is a status a person sets to park a run. It blocks nothing in the app (CS-013 §4).

sections.title: QR-007 Work orders: steps, buy-offs, holds and issues
sections.section: 6. Why is the demould (demold) step locked? Still curing
sections.text:
Cure and demould (or Cure) stays locked until the FEB hold has run from the finish time on the step before: 48 h IN2 + AT30 SLOW, 24 h FAST, 24 h West 206 or 205, 36 h West 209 (CS-008 §5). Sign early and you get "Still curing" (CS-013 §4; CS-008 §5.1).

Also called: demould, demold, de-mould, cure hold, FEB hold, wait time, still curing, locked, how long to cure, on hold, step on hold.

Signing the step that starts a cure ("Infuse", "Wet layup and bag", "Wet layup over core") asks for "Resin mixed", "Finished on" and "at", and "Shop temperature, °C (optional)". The next step stays locked until the FEB hold for that resin has run (CS-008 §5.1).

The FEB hold is longer than the datasheet figure on purpose. It is a team decision, signed off by Simon Starbuck on 2026-08-01, not a manufacturer claim (CS-008 §5.1). XCR's hold, the datasheet figures and the reasons are in QR-001 and CS-008 §5.1. On the step, the "why N h?" link explains the number.

If the recorded shop temperature is below the datasheet's reference, the app warns "Colder than this number assumes, so it will run long. Test the flange, not the clock." It leaves the hold unchanged (CS-008 §5.1).

Only a lead can sign through a hold, from "Demould early?", which asks "Why are you demoulding early?". The reason goes in the event log with the lead's name (CS-013 §4).

The hold reads only the step directly before it. A drop-test step placed between "Wet layup and bag" and "Cure and demould" would switch the hold off, so on a wet layup the drop test goes in the "Wet layup and bag" note (CS-007 §7.5).

sections.title: QR-007 Work orders: steps, buy-offs, holds and issues
sections.section: 7. What to do when something goes wrong: raising and closing an issue
sections.text:
Raise it on the run it holds up: ⚠ Raise an issue at the foot of the run's Issues section, or ⚑ (Report an issue on this step) on the step where it happened. Close it with a Disposition, What happened and What was done (CS-013 §7.6).

Also called: issue, ticket, problem, defect, NCR, nonconformance, disposition, scrap, rework, UAI, use as is.

1. Raise the issue with ⚠ Raise an issue, or ⚑ on the step.
2. To close it, open the run's Issues section, or the issue's page.
3. Pick a Disposition: UAI (Use As Is), Corrective Action, Rework, Scrap or Other.
4. Fill What happened, the root cause.
5. Fill What was done. Scrap asks "Why could it not be saved?"; UAI asks "Why is it acceptable as it is?".
6. Press Resolve (Resolve issue on the issue's page).

A false alarm is cancelled with Cancel ticket (false alarm), not disposed (CS-013 §7.6 step 4).

If a fix did not hold, press Reopen on the issue's page. It withdraws the disposition and clears What was done, keeps What happened, and the run is held again until the issue is disposed a second time (step 5).

A run shall not complete while any of its issues lacks a Disposition, What happened or What was done (step 3). The app checks only Disposition and What was done, so the person closing out checks What happened.

![The issue path on a run: raise it (⚠ Raise an issue, or ⚑ on a step), then Disposition, What happened and What was done; the app holds Complete until every issue has a Disposition and What was done. Reopen loops back and clears the disposition.](figures/cs013-issue-path.v2.png)

sections.title: QR-007 Work orders: steps, buy-offs, holds and issues
sections.text:
Fill the actuals in Quality (mass, thickness, Ω table), check the photos, and set the status to Complete. If an issue is still open, the app opens the closeout list instead; dispose each one (CS-013 §7.3).

Also called: close a work order, complete, finish a run, closeout, done, mark complete.

1. Fill the actuals in Quality: mass, thickness, Ω table and the rest.
2. Check the photos.
3. Set the status to Complete.
4. If the closeout list opens, press Resolve on each issue, or Resolve all & complete work order at the foot (CS-013 §7.6 step 3).
5. If the part is safety or inspection relevant, print one copy for the physical binder at RFS (CS-013 §7.3 step 3).

There is nothing to export by hand. Every save writes straight to the shared database (CS-013 §7.3 step 2). The archive is a lead's monthly Backup into the team Drive (header button; on a phone, Backup database in the ⋯ menu).

Which lots went in is asked at the infuse or wet layup buy-off: fabric roll, resin lot and hardener lot, pre-filled with whatever is open. "I don't know / not recorded" is a valid answer and is recorded as such. A confident wrong lot is worse than an honest gap (CS-013 §7.2 step 4).

sections.title: QR-007 Work orders: steps, buy-offs, holds and issues
sections.section: 9. I deleted something by mistake: Recently deleted
sections.text:
Go to Reports → Recently deleted and press Restore on the row. A deleted record stays there for 30 days, and restoring it brings back everything deleted with it, uploads included (CS-013 §7.7).

Also called: deleted, delete, undo delete, restore, bin, trash, recycle bin, recover, lost record; archive, archived.

1. Open the Reports tab.
2. Find the record under Recently deleted. Each row says who deleted it and how many days are left.
3. Press Restore.

Only a lead deletes parts, runs and issues. Deleting a run takes its issues and uploads with it (CS-013 §7.7 step 2). After 30 days a lead presses Empty them, and the records are gone for good (step 4). A deleted ID is never reissued (step 5).

A finished or abandoned part or run should be archived, not deleted (step 1). Any member can Archive one on its page in edit mode, or several with Select… on the list. An archived record leaves the lists, the Dashboard and the Season tab but keeps every field. The archived chip on the list shows them, each with Restore.

Delete is for a record that should never have existed (CS-013 §7.7 step 2).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 1. What PPE do I need for any epoxy resin or hardener?
sections.text:
Nitrile gloves, safety glasses with side shields (EN 166), ventilation, and soap (never solvent) on skin, for every resin and hardener the team stocks (CS-008 §6). All of them can make you allergic through the skin (H317), and every hardener burns skin and can blind (H314, H318).

Also called: epoxy PPE, resin safety, safety gear, gloves, nitrile, safety glasses, goggles, SDS, MSDS, safety sheet, sensitization, allergy.

- Gloves: nitrile, always, on both components and on mixed resin. Change them as soon as resin gets on them (CS-004 §6, CS-006 §6).
- Eyes: safety glasses with side shields whenever resin or hardener is open. Prescription glasses are not eye protection (CS-004 §6).
- Ventilation: work in the ventilated shop area or with doors open, not in a closed side room (CS-004 §6).
- Respirator: for long or enclosed sessions with any resin, wear the team respirator with the stocked A + P100 cartridges (CS-008 §6; CS-004 §6, CS-007 §6); IN2 and AT30 should get ABEK instead (CS-006 §6). Cartridges by job: QR-008 §14.
- No resin or hardener SDS on file classifies it as a respiratory sensitizer (no H334); the XCR SDS §11.1 still warns the resin may be one (CS-008 §6). Skin sensitization adds up: repeated careless exposure can make you permanently allergic to epoxies, which ends your composites career (CS-004 §6).
- If you have ever had a skin reaction to epoxy, tell a lead. You shall not mix or brush XCR (CS-004 §6).

QR-008 §2 to §5 add what each system's SDS asks for on top of this.

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 2. IN2 infusion resin and AT30 hardener: gloves, glasses, respirator
sections.text:
Nitrile gloves at all times once resin is out, and safety glasses with side shields (EN 166) whenever IN2 or AT30 is open (CS-006 §6). In a closed room or a long session, wear the team respirator with the stocked A + P100 cartridges (CS-006 §6; CS-008 §6). You should use ABEK cartridges (EN 14387) instead; they are on the purchase list.

Also called: IN2, infusion resin, infusion epoxy, AT30, AT30 SLOW, AT30 FAST, slow hardener, fast hardener, Easy Composites resin, EC resin.

What the SDS says (`03 Datasheets/EC-SDS-IN2-Epoxy-Infusion-Resin-and-Hardener.pdf`, quoted in CS-006 §6):

- IN2 resin irritates skin and eyes, causes allergic skin reactions and may damage fertility (H315, H319, H317, H360F).
- AT30, SLOW and FAST, is corrosive: severe skin burns and serious eye damage (H314, H318), allergic skin reactions (H317), harmful if swallowed (H302).
- AT30 FAST adds possible organ damage through repeated exposure (H373) and is corrosive to the respiratory tract (EUH071).

Handling (CS-006 §6):

- Change gloves after any contamination.
- Mix and infuse in the ventilated shop area; the SDS asks for effective ventilation in all processing areas. Sensitization is cumulative.
- IN2 may damage fertility (H360F). Anyone who is pregnant, trying to conceive or concerned should get medical advice before handling it (SDS P201, P308 + P313), and may ask a lead for other work without saying why.
- The shop stocks A + P100 cartridges (CS-011 §5), not ABEK, so A + P100 is required and ABEK is a should.
- Cut spiral-wrap ends pierce gloves and bags alike. Tape them.
- A full mixed pot of IN2 left standing overheats (CS-006 §6; QR-008 §12).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 3. XCR mold sealer: gloves, glasses and the respirator
sections.text:
Nitrile gloves always, safety glasses with side shields whenever XCR is open, and ventilation (CS-004 §6). For prolonged brushing on large molds, or poor ventilation, wear the team respirator with A1 (brown) cartridges. Seal in the open shop area or with doors open.

Also called: XCR, mold sealer, sealer, sealing resin, coating resin, epoxy coating resin, mould sealer.

What the SDS says (`03 Datasheets/EC-SDS-XCR-Epoxy-Coating-Resin-Combined.pdf`, quoted in CS-004 §6): resin and hardener both cause allergic skin reactions (H317) and serious eye damage (H318). The hardener causes severe skin burns (H314). The resin is suspected of causing genetic defects (H341). Neither is classified as a respiratory sensitizer (no H334), though SDS §11.1 says the resin may be one; the respirator is for vapor.

Rules (CS-004 §6):

- Anyone who has had a skin reaction to epoxy shall not mix or brush XCR, and tells a lead. There is other work on a sealing night.
- Gloves: nitrile (chemical-resistant per EN ISO 374-1), on both components and mixed resin. Change them if resin gets on them.
- Respirator: A-type (brown, EN 14387 A1) organic-vapor cartridges for undertray-scale molds or poor ventilation. Dust filters alone do nothing against epoxy vapors.
- Eyes: you should wear safety goggles with side protection (EN 166) when mixing or brushing XCR. Goggles are on the purchase list; until then, safety glasses with side shields.
- Skin: wash any contact at once with soap and water, not solvent. Contaminated clothing stays at the shop (XCR SDS P272).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 4. West System 105 and 205, 206, 209 hardeners: gloves, glasses, respirator
sections.text:
Nitrile gloves, safety glasses with side shields, ventilation and no solvent on skin; a respirator with an A-filter for large overhead or enclosed laminating (CS-007 §6, CS-008 §6). The hardeners are worse than the resin: all three burn skin and damage eyes.

Also called: West, West System, 105, 205, 206, 209, fast hardener, slow hardener, extra slow hardener, wet layup epoxy, laminating resin.

What the SDSs say (`03 Datasheets/WEST-SDS-105-Epoxy-Resin.pdf`, `WEST-SDS-205-Fast-Hardener.pdf`, `WEST-SDS-206-Slow-Hardener.pdf`, `WEST-SDS-209-Extra-Slow-Hardener.pdf`, quoted in CS-007 §6 and CS-008 §6):

| Product | Hazards for people |
|---|---|
| 105 resin | H315 skin irritation, H317 allergic skin reaction, H319 eye irritation |
| 205 fast hardener | H302, H312, H314, H317, H318, H341 suspected of causing genetic defects, H373 organ damage through repeated exposure |
| 206 slow hardener | H302, H314, H317, H318, H335 may irritate the lungs |
| 209 extra slow hardener | H302, H314, H317, H318, H335, H373 |

Handling:

- Wash skin with soap, never solvent (CS-008 §6).
- 105 with 205 in a pot gets hot fast. The exotherm rules apply (CS-007 §6; QR-008 §12).
- Treat 105 and its hardeners the way CS-008 §6 treats every resin system (QR-008 §1).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 5. DP420 structural adhesive: gloves, glasses, respirator
sections.text:
Nitrile gloves and safety glasses with side shields are required for DP420 mixing and bonding, and a respirator with OV/P100 cartridges when ventilation is not adequate (CS-009 §6). You should also wear indirect vented goggles and a full face shield, both on the purchase list.

Also called: DP420, DP 420, 3M DP420, Scotch-Weld, structural adhesive, structural epoxy, epoxy glue, two-part glue, cartridge glue, duo-pak.

Why: Part A causes severe skin burns and eye damage, which is why its SDS recommends goggles and a face shield (CS-009 §6, `03 Datasheets/3M-SDS-DP420-Black.pdf` Part A §8.2.2). The SDS rates nitrile and butyl gloves over 4 h for both parts (§8.2.2).

If Part A gets on you (DP420 SDS, Part A §4):

1. Skin: flush at once with large amounts of water for at least 15 minutes.
2. Take off contaminated clothing.
3. Get immediate medical attention.
4. Eyes: flush at once with large amounts of water for at least 15 minutes, removing contact lenses if that is easy, and get medical attention immediately.

Bond prep and the DP420 steps are in QR-013.

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 6. Acetone and IPA: which gloves, and how long they last
sections.text:
Nitrile gloves and safety glasses with side shields are required for a solvent wipe (CS-009 §6). Thin nitrile (0.11 mm) holds 100% IPA for 117 min, but acetone gets through even Ansell's 0.45 mm latex/neoprene/nitrile glove in 17 min (ASTM F739; 21 min by EN ISO 374): change gloves as soon as acetone wets them.

Also called: acetone, IPA, isopropyl alcohol, isopropanol, rubbing alcohol, 91% IPA, solvent, solvent wipe, cleaner, glove breakthrough, permeation.

Where the numbers come from: Ansell's charts, `03 Datasheets/ANSELL-chart-TouchNTuff-92-500-93-250.pdf` (0.11 mm nitrile) and `03 Datasheets/ANSELL-chart-TouchNTuff-93-800.pdf` (0.45 mm NRL/neoprene/nitrile), quoted in CS-009 §6. They test Ansell's gloves; the team's brand may differ.

- Respirator: none set. The solvent SDSs on file are stand-ins, so no number here comes from them (CS-009 §6).
- Wipe with ventilation, and put out ignition sources while solvents are open (CS-009 §6, §7.3).
- Acetone and 91% IPA are flammable (CS-014 §6). Acetone lives in the flammables cabinet (CS-011 §6). CS-011 §6 does not name IPA, and CS-004 §5 lists the 91% bottle in the Chemicals box.
- Never acetone on or near tooling board (CS-009 §7.3).
- On molds, use the 91% isopropyl bottle, never the 70% rubbing alcohol (CS-004 §5).
- Never use solvent to get resin off skin. Soap and water (CS-008 §6).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 7. Sanding and cutting dust: carbon, glass, G10 and tooling board
sections.text:
Cutting, sanding or machining cured CF, glass or G10 requires the dust extractor running at the cut, a half-facepiece respirator with OV/P100 cartridges, nitrile gloves, long sleeves, safety glasses with side shields, and a second trained person present (CS-009 §6).

Also called: dust, carbon dust, CF dust, fibre dust, fiber dust, sanding, cutting, trimming, Dremel, dust mask, P100, respirator, extractor, tooling board dust, board dust.

- CF dust is the team's worst routine exposure (CS-009 §6).
- Cut CF edges splinter. Gloves are for that as much as for the dust.
- Supervision (set in SN5; the Composites Lead may change it): no cutting cured carbon without a second trained person present. Trained means holding the Trimming and finishing training in the app (CS-009 §6). The lead adds that training in People → Catalog; until a lead has added and granted it, ask the lead who counts as trained.
- The shop stocks A + P100 cartridges; 3M 60921 is the OV/P100 cartridge on file (CS-009 §6, `03 Datasheets/3M-spec-60921-OV-P100-Cartridge.pdf`).
- Tooling-board dust (gluing prep, hand-shaping) is abrasive and irritating: a dust mask at minimum, a respirator and extraction for power sanding (CS-003 §6).
- On the ShopSabre: extraction on, a dust mask at minimum, a respirator for long jobs (CS-005 §6).
- Vacuum shared rooms. Do not blow dust around with compressed air (CS-005 §6).

Trimming and sanding steps are in QR-013.

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 8. Ure-Bond 90 tooling board glue: ventilation, gloves, respirator (isocyanate)
sections.text:
Glue only with room-size ventilation, and never heat or spray Ure-Bond 90. Wear safety glasses with side shields, long sleeves and gloves (CS-003 §6). Part A contains MDI, an isocyanate that may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled (H334). If the room cannot be ventilated, wear the CS-009 respirator (CS-003 §6).

- Asthma or a past reaction to isocyanates: you shall not mix Ure-Bond 90. Tell a lead; there is other work on a gluing night (CS-003 §6).
- Gloves: the SDS names liquid-tight butyl rubber, neoprene or PVC gloves, and the technical bulletin says rubber gloves; neither names nitrile. Until the shop stocks one of those, wear the shop's nitrile gloves. You should wear butyl, neoprene or PVC gloves; they are on the purchase list (CS-003 §6).

Also called: Ure-Bond, Urebond, Ure Bond 90, board glue, tooling board adhesive, urethane adhesive, Smooth-On, MDI, isocyanate, gluing the stack.

What the SDS says (`03 Datasheets/1386A_2-1386B_2.pdf`, quoted in CS-003 §6): Part A contains MDI (methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, CAS 101-68-8, 15 to 35 %). It causes skin and eye irritation, may cause an allergic skin reaction, is harmful if inhaled, may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled, may irritate the airways, is suspected of causing cancer and may damage the airways through repeated exposure (H315, H319, H317, H332, H334, H335, H351, H373). Part B is not classified.

- The technical bulletin warns the vapors become significant when heated or sprayed (`03 Datasheets/URE_BOND_90_TB.pdf`, CS-003 §6).
- Eyes: flush with water for 15 min and get medical attention (TB).
- Skin: remove with soap and water (TB).
- Clamped assemblies stay put for 4 h (TB).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 9. Clear coat (LiME LiNE UC4:1): Part B stays shut
sections.text:
Nobody opens, mixes or applies Part B, the isocyanate activator, until its SDS or the can's hazard text is in `03 Datasheets/` and CS-009 §6 quotes its PPE. For Part A, a respirator with OV/P100 cartridges and nitrile gloves are required (CS-009 §6).

Also called: clear coat, clearcoat, clear, LiME LiNE, Lime Line, UC4:1, urethane clear, activator, Part B, GH60, GH70, GH80.

Part A (`03 Datasheets/LIMELINE-SDS-UC4-1-Clearcoat-Part-A.pdf`, quoted in CS-009 §6):

- Hazards: highly flammable liquid and vapor (H225), may cause an allergic skin reaction (H317), serious eye irritation (H319), may cause drowsiness or dizziness (H336).
- Use it only outdoors or in a well-ventilated area.
- Eyes: you should wear tightly sealed goggles, which are on the purchase list. Until then, safety glasses with side shields.
- Respirator: the OV/P100 respirator covers brief exposure. For intensive or longer exposure the SDS asks for a respirator independent of circulating air; the team sets that when Part B's PPE is quoted (CS-009 §7.4 step 1).
- Gloves: nitrile. The SDS names no glove material.
- Part A is flammable (CS-014 §6) and lives in the flammables cabinet (CS-011 §6).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 10. Airtac 2 spray adhesive: flammable, how to spray it safely
sections.text:
Airtac 2 is an extremely flammable aerosol: no sparks or heat, use it in a ventilated space, and spray in short bursts (CS-006 §6). The SDS on file, the 2005 MSDS of the earlier Airtac 2 Spray Adhesive (a current one is wanted, CS-006 R5), classes it as a Class IA flammable liquid with a flash point of −42 °F (CS-014 §6), so it is stored in the flammables cabinet (CS-011 §6).

Also called: Airtac, Air Tac, Airtac 2, tack spray, spray tack, spray adhesive, spray glue, Airtech spray.

- SDS: `03 Datasheets/airtac2spray.pdf`.
- Use a light mist only, from at least 30 cm (CS-006 §5).
- When it arrives, set the lot's Hazard to flammable (CS-014 §6).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 11. Mold release wax, PVA, graphite powder and copper mesh
sections.text:
Release wax and PVA are low hazard: gloves and ventilation suffice (CS-004 §6). Graphite powder needs the respirator with a P100 cartridge and nitrile gloves while you weigh and mix it (CS-010 §6). Cut copper mesh has sharp wire ends: wear gloves to cut and place it.

Also called: wax, Formula Five, release wax, PVA, Partall, release film, graphite, graphite powder, conductive powder, copper mesh, grounding mesh.

- Wax and PVA: Formula Five Mold Release Wax and Partall Film #10 (CS-004 §5). Their SDSs are `03 Datasheets/SDS-F5MRW-5.3-en-NA-2025-01-28.pdf` and `03 Datasheets/SDS-PF10-5.5-en-NA-2025-01-28.pdf`.
- Graphite: the shop stocks A + P100 cartridges and nitrile gloves, so both are required (CS-010 §6). No graphite SDS is on file yet.
- Copper mesh: gloves when cutting and placing it (CS-010 §6).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 12. A mixing cup is getting hot or smoking (exotherm)
sections.text:
A warm cup: use it at once or spread it thin. A hot or smoking cup: carry it outside onto concrete and leave it. Do not bin it and do not dilute it with water indoors. Nothing goes in the trash until it is fully cured and cool (CS-008 §6).

Also called: hot cup, hot pot, exotherm, smoking cup, runaway, cooking off, kicking off, cup going off.

Mass concentrated in a cup speeds the cure up, and the cure's own heat speeds it up again (CS-008 §4, §6). To stop it happening:

1. Mix the smallest batch that does the job (CS-008 §6).
2. Pour out of the pot promptly (CS-008 §6).
3. Spread leftovers thin on scrap, or leave them outside to cure (CS-008 §7 step 7).

Which systems bite fastest: 105 with 205 in a pot gets hot fast (CS-007 §6); mixed XCR left in the pot self-accelerates (CS-004 §6); a full mixed pot of IN2 left standing overheats (CS-006 §6).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 13. Resin or hardener on skin or in an eye: first aid
sections.text:
In an eye: rinse with plenty of water, under the eyelids too, for at least 15 minutes, then get medical attention (CS-008 §6). On skin: wash it off at once with soap and plenty of water, never solvents or thinners (IN2 SDS §4).

Also called: first aid, splash, eye wash, eyewash, rinse, chemical burn, skin contact, rash, allergic reaction, dermatitis.

Eye:

1. Rinse with plenty of water at once.
2. Hold the eyelids open and rinse under them.
3. Take out contact lenses if that is easy, and keep rinsing (West 105 SDS, P305+351+338).
4. Keep rinsing for at least 15 minutes (CS-008 §6).
5. Get medical attention.

Skin:

1. Take off contaminated clothing (XCR SDS, P303+P361+P353). It stays at the shop (CS-004 §6).
2. Wash with soap and plenty of water. No solvent (`03 Datasheets/EC-SDS-IN2-Epoxy-Infusion-Resin-and-Hardener.pdf` §4).
3. DP420 Part A on skin: flush for at least 15 minutes and get immediate medical attention (DP420 SDS, Part A §4; QR-008 §5).
4. A rash or other skin reaction afterwards: tell a lead. You shall not mix or brush XCR again (CS-004 §6).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 14. Which respirator cartridge for which job?
sections.text:
Dust, DP420 in poor ventilation and clear coat Part A take OV/P100 cartridges; the shop stocks A + P100 (CS-009 §6, required). XCR and West vapor take A-type cartridges. AT30 should get ABEK, which is on the purchase list (CS-006 §6).

Also called: respirator, mask, cartridge, filter, organic vapor, OV, OV/P100, P100, A1, ABEK, 60921, half mask, half-facepiece.

| Job | Cartridge | Rule | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cutting, sanding or machining cured CF, glass, G10 | OV/P100, half-facepiece | Required | CS-009 §6 |
| DP420, ventilation not adequate | OV/P100 | Required | CS-009 §6 |
| Clear coat Part A | OV/P100 | Required | CS-009 §6 |
| Graphite powder | P100 | Required | CS-010 §6 |
| XCR, prolonged brushing on large molds or poor ventilation | A1 (brown) | Wear it | CS-004 §6 |
| West, large overhead or enclosed laminating | A-filter | Wear it | CS-007 §6 |
| IN2 and AT30, closed room or long session | A + P100 | Required | CS-006 §6, CS-008 §6 |
| IN2 and AT30, closed room or long session | ABEK | Should (purchase list) | CS-006 §6 |
| Ure-Bond 90, room cannot be ventilated | The CS-009 respirator | Required | CS-003 §6 |
| Solvent wipe (IPA, acetone) | None set | | CS-009 §6 |

Required means PPE the shop stocks, which the standards make a shall. Should means PPE an SDS asks for that the shop does not stock yet; each of those items is on the purchase list (Simon, 2026-10-10).

Dust filters alone do nothing against epoxy vapors (CS-004 §6). The shop's restock list carries A + P100 cartridges (CS-011 §5).

sections.title: QR-008 PPE and handling by chemical
sections.section: 15. Where do chemicals get stored, and what if one leaks?
sections.text:
Resins and hardeners go in the chemical boxes or barrel, never in a food fridge; flammables (Airtac, acetone, clear coat) go in the flammables cabinet (CS-011 §6). A leaking container never goes on a shelf: keep it in its packaging, set it apart and tell a lead (CS-014 §6).

Also called: chemical storage, storing resin, flammables cabinet, fridge, leak, spill, damaged container, unpacking a delivery.

Co-storage: see CS-011 §6; under review.

CS-011 §6 as it stands also says to segregate hardeners from resins on different shelves.

Unpacking a delivery (CS-014 §6):

1. Wear nitrile gloves to unpack and shelve chemical containers.
2. Before you touch a damaged or leaking container, read its SDS.
3. Leave a leaking container in its packaging, apart from other chemicals, and tell a lead. The lead decides what happens to it.
4. Put chemicals straight onto a location CS-011 §6 allows. Never a fridge.

Which site is which, and how to record a move, is in QR-014.

sections.title: QR-009 Words the team uses
sections.section: 1. Car and part names: what do UT, RW and FW mean?
sections.text:
UT is the undertray, RW the rear wing and FW the front wing. SN5 is the team's fifth car and SN6 the sixth; the season code is the middle of every ID, as in `P-SN6-007`, and SN5 IDs stay frozen (CS-013 §4.1).

Also called: UT, undertray, under tray, floor; RW, rear wing, wing; FW, front wing; SN5, SN6, the car; aero parts.

- Undertray (UT): the inlet, the diffuser, the left and right side pods, the strakes and the air dams.
- Rear wing (RW): the elements and the endplates. The RW E2 to E5 elements are the foam-wrapped class of part (CS-007 §7.7).
- Front wing (FW).
- Other composites parts: nosecone, clamshell, dashboard, seat, steering wheel, catch can.
- Catch can: the SN5 part with carbon over a thin metal can, the cautionary tale for sanding through and for grounding (CS-009 §1, CS-010 §7.1).
- Forged CF: compression-molded carbon, made in 3D-printed molds (CS-003 Appendix A).
- Aero parts are often defined in #aerodynamics; composites builds them.

sections.title: QR-009 Words the team uses
sections.section: 2. Mold and tooling board words: flange, scribe line, mold file, stage
sections.text:
A mold is cut on the ShopSabre from tooling board glued into a stack. The flange is the flat margin round the cavity for tacky tape and lines, and scribe lines are machined V-grooves marking the trim line and datums (CS-003 §4).

Also called: mold, mould, tool; tooling board, board, Precision Board, PBLT; stack, block, mold stock, blank; flange; scribe line, etch line, trim line.

- Stack (mold stock): tooling boards glued into a block thick enough for the mold. Not the same as a layup stack (QR-009 §10).
- Mold record: `MOLD-SN6-###`, on the Molds tab, from the moment the stack is planned.
- Mold file: the mold's current stack plan, `STK-SN6-###`. Older plans show under Earlier, marked Superseded.
- Mold stage: Designed, Tooling cut, Board glued, Machined, Sealed, Ready for layup; Retired sits off the track. A mold that will not be used again is retired, never deleted.
- Datum cut plan: the drawing of reference cuts taken off a mold after a part comes out. Most molds never need one.
- Sealing: closing the open cells of machined board so resin cannot soak in and lock the part on. XCR does it (CS-004 §4).
- Release system: wax, then PVA film, between the sealed mold and the part.
- B-stage, firm-but-tacky: resin firm enough not to flow but soft enough to dent with a fingernail; the right time to overcoat (CS-004 §4).

sections.title: QR-009 Words the team uses
sections.section: 3. Bagging consumables: peel ply, breather, flow mesh, tacky tape
sections.text:
Peel ply is the release fabric on the laminate, breather the lofted cloth under the bag, flow mesh the green mesh that spreads resin in an infusion, and tacky tape seals the bag to the flange (CS-006 §5, CS-007 §4).

Also called: consumables; peel ply, release ply, PP180; breather, bleeder, batting; flow mesh, infusion mesh, flow media, green mesh, 2-in-1 mesh; tacky tape, sealant tape, AT-200Y, yellow tape; bag, vacuum bag, VB160, bag film; spiral, spiral wrap; resin trap, catch pot.

- Bag film: VB160 (CS-006 §5).
- Peel ply: PP180, or Sigmatex-supplied (CS-006 §5).
- Breather: gives air a path to the vacuum port and soaks up excess resin. Kept clear of part edges, where it glues on (CS-007 §4).
- Flow mesh: covers the whole part in an infusion. The 2-in-1 mesh is mesh and peel ply in one (CS-006 §5).
- Tacky tape: Airtech AT-200Y (yellow) sealant tape (CS-006 §5).
- Spiral wrap and PE tubing: the feed and vacuum lines (CS-006 §5).
- Resin trap, catch pot: the sealed pot between the bag outlet and the pump that catches over-pulled resin. Without it the first overlong pull kills the pump (CS-006 §4).
- Pleats: folds built into the bag with tacky tape so the film reaches into corners (CS-006 §4).
- Bridging: bag film spanning a corner instead of following it. It punctures or leaves a resin-rich void (CS-007 §4).

sections.title: QR-009 Words the team uses
sections.section: 4. Infusion and wet layup words: drop test, inHg, wet-out, race-tracking
sections.text:
A drop test (leak-down) shuts the bag off from the pump and watches the gauge, to find leaks before resin goes in. inHg, inches of mercury, is what the team's vacuum gauges read; full vacuum at sea level is about 29.9 inHg (CS-006 §4).

Also called: drop test, leak test, leak-down, leak check; inHg, inches of mercury, vacuum, vac; infusion, infuse, VARTM, resin infusion; wet layup, wet lay, hand layup; wet-out, wetting out; race-tracking, racing.

- Nothing reads "30 psi of vacuum": atmospheric pressure is only about 14.7 psi. A gauge showing psi is reading something else (CS-006 §4).
- Race-tracking: resin finding a fast path, usually along an edge, and reaching the outlet before the middle is wet (CS-006 §4).
- Wet-out: cloth fully saturated, a uniform sheen with the weave still visible. Swimming in resin is past wet-out, not better (CS-007 §4).
- 60:40: the target cured fiber to resin ratio, by weight (CS-007 §4).
- Infusion: the dry stack is bagged and resin is pulled through it under vacuum (CS-006). Wet layup: plies are wetted by hand, then bagged (CS-007).
- Foam wrapped: wet plies wrapped round a shaped foam core instead of laid in a mold (CS-007 §7.7).
- Double-pot: mix, pour into a second cup, mix again with a fresh stick (CS-008 §7 step 3).
- Degas, degassing: an optional step that pulls the air out of mixed IN2 under vacuum before it is infused (CS-006 §7.8).

sections.title: QR-009 Words the team uses
sections.section: 5. Resin names: IN2, AT30, West, XCR, DP420
sections.text:
IN2 with AT30 hardener is the infusion resin, West System 105 with 205, 206 or 209 is the wet layup resin, XCR seals molds, and DP420 is the structural adhesive. Ratios and holds per system are in CS-008 §5 and QR-001.

Also called: resin, epoxy, hardener, activator, Part B; IN2, infusion resin; AT30, AT30 SLOW, AT30 FAST; West, West System, 105, 205 fast, 206 slow, 209 extra slow; XCR, sealer, coating resin; DP420, 3M glue, structural adhesive; 404, filler, thickened epoxy; clear coat, LiME LiNE.

- IN2 and AT30 come from Easy Composites (EC). AT30 comes in SLOW and FAST (CS-008 §5).
- West 105 is the resin; 205, 206 and 209 are its hardeners. 206 is the wet layup default (CS-008 §5).
- 209 uses 3:1 pumps, not the 5:1 pumps of 205 and 206: the classic wrong-ratio trap (CS-008 §7 step 1).
- XCR: Easy Composites' epoxy coating resin for mold sealing (CS-004).
- DP420: 3M Scotch-Weld structural adhesive in a duo-pak cartridge (CS-009 §5).
- West 404: high-density filler for thickened epoxy, for fillets and gap filling (CS-009 §5).
- LiME LiNE UC4:1: the urethane clear coat (CS-009 §5).
- Ure-Bond 90: the tooling-board glue, a urethane (CS-003 §6).
- Airtac 2: the spray tack for holding carbon and mesh on a mold (CS-006 §5).

sections.title: QR-009 Words the team uses
sections.section: 6. Cure words: pot life, gel, demould (demold), FEB hold, full cure, exotherm
sections.text:
The FEB hold is how long the team waits before demoulding, and it governs. It is longer than the datasheet figure on purpose and is a team decision, not a manufacturer claim (CS-008 §5.1). Pot life is the usable time in the cup (CS-008 §4).

Also called: demould, demold, de-mould, demoulding, demolding; FEB hold, cure hold, team hold, wait time; pot life, working time, open time; gel, gelled, kicked; full cure; exotherm, hot cup.

- Pot life: usable time in the mixing pot, at the mass and temperature the TDS states. A bigger batch or a warmer shop shortens it (CS-008 §4).
- Gel: the resin no longer flows. Gel is not cure; a gelled part pried off a mold drags resin with it (CS-008 §4).
- Demould: the earliest the part can leave the mold without damage (CS-008 §4).
- Datasheet cure figure: the manufacturer's number, at their temperature. FEB hold: the team's number, which the app enforces on the step after the cure starts (CS-008 §5.1).
- Full cure: full mechanical properties. Weeks, not hours, for every system (CS-008 §4).
- Exotherm: the cure's own heat. Mass in a cup speeds it up (CS-008 §4).
- Still curing: what the app says when you try to sign a held step early (CS-013 §4).
- Demould early?: the lead's way to sign through a hold, with a written reason (CS-008 §5.1).

sections.title: QR-009 Words the team uses
sections.section: 7. What do the ID prefixes mean? WO, P, MOLD, RDS, CPN, STK
sections.text:
Every record ID reads `PREFIX-SNx-###`. WO is a work order, P a part, MOLD a mold, RDS an R&D study, CPN a coupon, STK a mold's stack plan (CS-013 §4.1). IDs are never reused.

Also called: ID, part number, P number, WO number, record ID, prefix, code.

| Prefix | What it names |
|---|---|
| `WO` | a work order (the job) |
| `P` | a part |
| `MOLD` | a mold |
| `PNL` | a flat test panel |
| `BRD` | a tooling-board sheet or offcut |
| `FAB` | a fabric roll or usable offcut |
| `RSN` | a resin or hardener lot |
| `CON` | a consumable lot |
| `JIG` | a jig or fixture |
| `BIN` | a storage location |
| `RDS` | an R&D study: a named set of coupons |
| `CPN` | one coupon, a single test piece in a study |
| `PROJ` | an issue (older records say ticket); no label |
| `STK` | a mold's stack plan, the Mold file; no label |
| `BUY` | a purchase; no label |
| `DOC` | a document on the Documents tab; no label |

- An ID names a physical object, never a job; `WO` is the one exception (CS-013 §4.1 rule 1).
- An ID is capped at 14 characters by the QR code (CS-013 §4.1).
- Dates are fields, never part of an ID.
- A re-laid part keeps its `P` ID and gets a new run (CS-013 §4.1 rule 3; QR-009 §8).

sections.title: QR-009 Words the team uses
sections.section: 8. Work order words: run, buy-off, blocker, cure hold, technique, issue
sections.text:
A run is one attempt at making a part; the app's Work Orders tab calls a run a work order (CS-013 §4). A buy-off is pressing a step's sign-off while signed in. A blocker step blocks everything after it until it is signed.

Also called: WO, work order, run, job, traveler, traveller; buy-off, sign-off, sign, signing; blocker, locked step, gate; cure hold, hold; technique, checklist, process, layup type; issue, ticket, ⚑, disposition; retro WO.

- Part and run: a part (`P-SNx-###`) is the durable thing the car needs, and it has many runs (CS-013 §4).
- Blockers: Stack frozen, Mold design review, the drop test, and the acceptance criterion of the Other technique (CS-013 §4).
- Evidence: what a step needs before it can be signed, such as a layup stack, the CAD, or a note (CS-013 §4).
- Training to sign: a step only someone holding the named training may sign. A lead may sign without it and must write why (CS-013 §4).
- Cure hold: the wait on the step after the one that starts a cure, as long as the FEB hold for the resin recorded (CS-013 §4).
